An attacker could repeatedly POST to the same reachable valid webhook path with an invalid or missing secret while varying ?nonce=..., causing every 401 to create and retain a distinct webhookStatusCounters entry and eventually exert memory pressure or trigger OOM. The similarly raw-URL-keyed rate-limit map was also unbounded, although that path ran only after successful target authentication; the unauthenticated advisory path is the 401 status-counter insertion.
causal_chain.flaw_origin: Commit a23e0d5140e5126f5055a46824cae4ba0a097ba3 added Zalo webhook ingress hardening, including anomaly accounting and rate limiting. In extensions/zalo/src/monitor.ts it introduced webhookStatusCounters as an unbounded Map, recordWebhookStatus() as an unconditional insertion for security error statuses, and calls that passed req.url for pre-authentication 401 responses. This composed a normalized route match with attacker-controlled raw-URL keying and unbounded retention; later commit 453664f09d0911cc1829d22c63f664f0ad2c8c10 only moved the already-vulnerable logic into monitor.webhook.ts.

reasoning: The vulnerability is in the Git node's original trust model, not in a later move or refactor. The staged repository controls Git remote metadata; push to a local crafted target enters Git's receive side and can run target hooks in the n8n process. Later path checks and core.hooksPath hardening narrowed other routes but left this local write transport reachable, so they do not replace the original BIC. The main-history commit 3667b0dd01f82046549b795b98b88983bd7c7fbb is a squash aggregate, and treating it as the BIC would violate the protocol because PR #1820's retained commit objects reconstruct the smaller member. Member f81e76aca958dab7392942e8a74b7919e7db42b5 is the earliest member and already contains both causal ingredients: attacker-selected local baseDirectory and unrestricted `git.push()`. Its immediate parent lacks the Git node path, while later members merely expand operations (for example pushTags) or refine the node. The patch lifecycle and exact tag boundaries corroborate this mechanism: the decisive remediation disables local file transport for write operations when hooks are not enabled. AI attribution is therefore judged only on f81e76aca958dab7392942e8a74b7919e7db42b5; its commit object is human-authored/committed and has no AI trailer. AI/bot markers on the 2026 fix bundles are irrelevant to BIC attribution, yielding NOT_AI.

causal_chain.bug_semantics: The Git node accepted an attacker-selected local repository and ran push/pushTags while Git's file transport remained permitted. An authenticated workflow author could stage repository metadata whose configured local target was a crafted repository containing receive hooks; the local git-receive-pack path then executed those hooks as the n8n process. The later default core.hooksPath=/dev/null mitigation covered hooks for the invoking repository but did not make a write to an attacker-controlled local target safe. The fix validates configured remotes and, when hooks are disabled, removes file from GIT_ALLOW_PROTOCOL specifically for push and pushTags.
causal_chain.flaw_origin: The first Git node implementation trusted repository-controlled local configuration and destination selection: it constructed simple-git with a workflow-supplied baseDirectory and exposed git.push() without restricting local remote targets or the file transport. causal_chain.bug_semantics: A malicious repository can put traversal components in a .gitmodules section name. GitPython parses that attacker-controlled section name without validation, assigns it to Submodule._name, and during Submodule.update(init=True) uses it to form <parent git dir>/modules/<name>. The resulting escaped path is passed to directory and clone operations, so initialization creates an attacker-controlled Git repository outside the intended clone directory.
causal_chain.flaw_origin: Commit 503b62bd76ee742bd18a1803dac76266fa8901bc introduced _module_abspath() with os.path.join(parent_repo.git_dir, 'modules', name) and changed the initialization branch of Submodule.update() from the tree-backed submodule path to this unchecked name-derived path before Repo.clone_from(). That is the first causal connection between an untrusted .gitmodules name and the filesystem repository-creation sink; the pre-existing unchecked sm_name() parser alone did not create this attack path.

At 503b62bd76ee742bd18a1803dac76266fa8901bc, git/objects/submodule/util.py sm_name() returns section[11:-1] unchecked; git/objects/submodule/base.py iter_items() reads n = sm_name(sms) and assigns sm._name = n. The same commit adds _module_abspath() at then-lines 204-210, whose Git-file branch returns os.path.join(parent_repo.git_dir, 'modules', name).

The 503b62bd76ee742bd18a1803dac76266fa8901bc diff changes the Submodule.update() initialization branch from module_path = join_path_native(self.repo.working_tree_dir, self.path) to module_path = self._module_abspath(self.repo, self.path, self.name), after which Repo.clone_from(self.url, module_path, n=True) creates the repository. The path value in the parent was constrained by the required pc.tree[path] lookup; the newly used section name was not validated.

reasoning: The advisory's security boundary is origin isolation, not merely the presence of raw HTML. The earlier 7ea920dbe742c0ca7c79c9df749aa7d7c898c571 allowed intentional custom HTML and script but coupled it to an unconditional sandbox CSP; the immediate parent of 7f651ca5a3162ba0f13242dc934047e32998b33c still had that guard. The BIC introduced a mode-dependent CSP exception without coupling responseText to showText. Because n8n parameters can resolve from expressions, respondWith could evaluate to redirect while a saved responseText remained populated; the template then chose and rendered responseText instead of the redirect UI, now without the sandbox. The August 2026 fix closes precisely that data/control mismatch by blanking responseText unless respondWith is showText, and the three backports align exactly with the advisory's patched tag boundaries. The BIC is an ordinary single-parent commit rather than a squash requiring member decomposition. Its commit object provides human authorship and no AI attribution; later bot-authored aggregate fix carriers are irrelevant under the BIC-only attribution rule. The causal and attribution evidence therefore closes as NOT_AI.

causal_chain.bug_semantics: An authenticated n8n member could preserve attacker-controlled responseText containing script while making the Form node's expression-evaluated respondWith resolve to redirect. renderFormCompletion loaded responseText regardless of the selected response mode, omitted the sandbox Content-Security-Policy whenever respondWith was redirect, and passed both values to a Handlebars completion template that preferred responseText and emitted it with triple braces. A visitor submitting the public form therefore received the attacker's raw HTML without the sandbox and the script executed from the n8n origin with the visitor's session context.
causal_chain.flaw_origin: The mechanism was assembled in two steps. Commit 7ea920dbe742c0ca7c79c9df749aa7d7c898c571 intentionally stopped sanitizing responseText but simultaneously installed an unconditional sandbox CSP, so it did not yet create the advisory's same-origin execution path. Commit 7f651ca5a3162ba0f13242dc934047e32998b33c then made that CSP conditional on respondWith not being redirect while leaving responseText loaded and rendered independently of respondWith. That guard removal is the smallest commit that completed the vulnerable combination.

Doubling caller-controlled backslashes before gm performs its quote escaping prevents a crafted backslash from neutralizing gm's escape; the installed-font allowlist closes the adjacent attacker-controlled font path. causal_chain.bug_semantics: The authenticated workflow-controlled Edit Image Draw Text operation word-wraps its text parameter and passes the resulting string to gm.drawText(). gm 1.23.1 constructs a quoted GraphicsMagick MVG -draw argument and escapes double quotes, but it does not escape backslashes already supplied by the caller. An attacker can place a backslash immediately before a quote so gm's added backslash is itself escaped, closing the intended MVG text primitive and allowing a following attacker-selected MVG primitive to make a blind outbound request or open a local file.

causal_chain.bug_semantics: search_files checked the literal user-supplied glob for a slash-delimited '..' segment before calling fast-glob, but did not validate the paths produced by glob expansion. A pattern such as '{a,..}/SECRET.txt' contains no literal '..' segment, passes the check, and can expand to '../SECRET.txt'; the tool then joined that result to the resolved working directory and either returned the outside filename or read matching lines from the outside file, disclosing files readable by the n8n OS user.
causal_chain.flaw_origin: PR #30670 replaced the parent implementation's bounded readdir-based collectFiles traversal with fastGlob(name, { cwd: resolvedDir }) and added only assertPatternStaysInside(name). The new pre-expansion lexical check rejected explicit absolute paths and literal '..' segments, but the result path was consumed by path.join(resolvedDir, fp) without post-expansion canonicalization or containment checking. That change first created the advisory's path-confinement bypass.

causal_chain.bug_semantics: CredentialsPermissionChecker builds the set of credential IDs to authorize by filtering node.credentials against credential-type names inferred statically from unresolved node parameters. For an HTTP Request node, an attacker with edit access to a shared workflow can put another user's known credential ID under its real credential type while setting genericAuthType to an expression. The pre-execution checker sees the expression source string rather than the runtime-resolved type, so the real credential key is omitted from the authorization query; execution later resolves the expression and loads/uses that credential, enabling unauthorized use or exfiltration.

Squash landing 608e3bf214328e679c03da3e4a6e9c22ceaac9ca carried that flaw. Later bundle 2d9a2ec76e180b54e8091e31b1e0638c909abd99 added genericAuthType to the static set, fixing literal generic types but preserving the advisory's expression form because it inserted the unresolved expression literal rather than the resolved credential type.

causal_chain.bug_semantics: A user who can configure a Budibase automation can supply an arbitrary HTTP(S) URL to the outgoing-webhook (and later Zapier, n8n, Slack, Discord, and Make.com) step. The server dereferenced that URL with axios/node-fetch without destination validation, so it could reach loopback, RFC1918, link-local/cloud-metadata, and other internal services (CWE-918). The REST datasource's separate guard was also fail-open by default because an unset BLACKLIST_IPS produced an empty list and isBlacklisted returned false; it neither protected automation fetches nor supplied secure defaults.
causal_chain.flaw_origin: Commit 3ae82b95a31bcb6b3803d3ad8d8c5accb7606ef3 first created and registered the executable OUTGOING_WEBHOOK automation. Its run function accepted inputs.url, normalized it only by adding http://, and called axios(request) with no allowlist/denylist or resolved-address check. Commit 3d77163773d0ab37342e9e2be5d6b8797758e4eb later changed axios to node-fetch, and a3bb2e0d770fe0c66f0382aebef86faa2bbcc696 renamed/migrated the same step to TypeScript; those are implementation changes preserving the pre-existing SSRF, not introducers. Commit 564c724be11895fa6bc1766aef3a149fae3223e3 later added an opt-in REST-only blacklist whose empty-default behavior left that separate path unprotected when BLACKLIST_IPS was unset.

The subsequent OpenFile call uses O_CREATE|O_TRUNC, so the OS follows the dangling symlink and creates the target outside the scope.

causal_chain.bug_semantics: TemplateContext.Reset() made a context appear safe to reuse but left its CachedTemplates dictionary intact. After one render cached a request-dependent include, a later render on the reset context found the same path in CachedTemplates and returned the old compiled Template without invoking ITemplateLoader.Load(), so content authorized for an earlier request, user, or tenant could cross the reuse boundary.
causal_chain.flaw_origin: Commit 2e95889099c3ee5e7a4c0147b7355ecd309200af introduced the public Reset() API and explicitly promised safe same-thread reuse, but reset only output, global, culture, and source-file stacks. Scriban's include cache and loader-on-cache-miss path already existed in the immediate parent; omitting CachedTemplates from the newly defined reset boundary is therefore the smallest change that created the advisory's vulnerable lifecycle.

causal_chain.bug_semantics: TemplateContext caches an IObjectAccessor solely under the target's System.Type. For ordinary .NET objects, the cached TypedObjectAccessor eagerly computes its member dictionary using the context's then-current MemberFilter (and MemberRenamer). If the same TemplateContext is later reused after MemberFilter is tightened, GetMemberAccessor returns the permissive accessor already cached for that Type, so reads or writes of members now denied by policy remain available.
causal_chain.flaw_origin: ace7a0ebafa6d01500f83c35975cde38d559fa3d first added TemplateContext.MemberFilter and, in the same commit, passed that mutable per-context policy into TypedObjectAccessor while leaving the pre-existing Type-only _memberAccessors cache unchanged and without invalidation. causal_chain.bug_semantics: POST /api/provider-nodes/validate accepts caller-controlled baseUrl and apiKey, makes server-side requests to baseUrl-derived provider endpoints, and forwards the supplied secret in Authorization headers. The later assertPublicUrl mitigation checks only the URL hostname string: it neither resolves DNS nor revalidates redirect destinations, and its IPv4-mapped IPv6 regex expects a dotted quad even though WHATWG URL canonicalization has already converted that quad to hextets. A mapped loopback or link-local literal, a domain resolving to a private address, or a redirect can therefore reach internal services. The custom-embedding path reflects the first 200 bytes of a non-2xx response other than 401/403; the other paths expose status, timing, and error differences for blind port scanning.
causal_chain.flaw_origin: Commit 0a28f9f924d2dc53027a910679ee3cff3e63a59c created the validation route and, in the same minimal change, read baseUrl/apiKey from the request, interpolated baseUrl into /models, fetched it without any destination policy, and forwarded apiKey as a Bearer token. That is the first complete attacker-controlled outbound-request mechanism. Commit 0b8bed5793c7a7c9beb7a5db7368720907f61ebc later added the custom-embedding branch and 200-byte error-body disclosure; 090886ced9a3481837f5687ec66da7d9f33eea08 later connected a hostname-only guard; and 8ac631d6158c0f04976a0d0f7ca9ec2b981efeb5 later added an ineffective mapped-IPv6 check. Those later changes altered impact or attempted mitigation but did not originate the SSRF sink, which was already exploitable in their parents.

causal_chain.bug_semantics: A browser page can retain the attacker-controlled origin name while DNS rebinding moves its TCP connection to Paperclip on loopback. Paperclip accepted the attacker hostname because the API had no Host-header gate, assigned requests without a valid bearer credential the trusted board actor, allowed that actor to create/configure an agent, and exposed a heartbeat invocation path whose process adapter passed the stored command and arguments to node:child_process spawn. Thus visiting an attacker page could turn an unauthenticated cross-origin web request into command execution as the Paperclip OS user.
causal_chain.flaw_origin: abadd469bc85e9fa5137ff5ffce433f1c2db2c0b is the smallest commit that completed the RCE mechanism. In one non-merge commit it added server/src/middleware/auth.ts with a board actor as the default for requests lacking a recognized bearer key, mounted company and expanded agent routes in server/src/app.ts without any Host validation, added agent creation and POST /agents/:id/heartbeat/invoke, and created server/src/services/heartbeat.ts where non-HTTP adapter configuration supplies command, args, cwd, and env to spawn(). Its immediate parent had the basic API shell but neither heartbeat.ts nor this process-execution path, so it could not execute an API-configured local command through the disclosed chain.

causal_chain.bug_semantics: The runner registration-token API exposed token creation through GET routes. The existing token-scope middleware derives Read versus Write solely from the HTTP method, so a read-scoped user, organization, repository, or admin token could pass the GET route even though shared.GetRegistrationToken calls actions_model.NewRunnerToken when no usable token exists. The caller receives that credential and can register an Actions runner, which can then execute workflow jobs with access to repository source and secrets.

A later member, bba250f3e99bef12bbd9a1d9d790ab8155c999d5, added the user and repository variants, extending rather than originating the same flawed mechanism.

causal_chain.bug_semantics: An authenticated non-site-admin with the perm_template permission can GET the event-template add page (or edit a template writable by that user's organisation). EventTemplatesController::__setBuilderConfig() queried every enabled Galaxy row without Galaxy visibility conditions, grouped the results by type, retained each type and description, and embedded that data in window.ET_BUILDER_CONFIG.multipickerSources. Consequently, the builder response disclosed metadata for enabled private distribution-0 galaxies owned by other organisations.
causal_chain.flaw_origin: Commit 47bf71cc78d13c06e1eaa4d9842e6f94ddce4bea introduced the galaxy-type picker and, in the same atomic feature commit, first added the server-side Galaxy->find('all') with only 'Galaxy.enabled' => true. It did not call Galaxy::buildConditions() or otherwise restrict by the requesting user's organisation/distribution before exposing Galaxy.type and Galaxy.description to the browser.

git log -S"'Galaxy.enabled' => true" -- app/Controller/EventTemplatesController.php resolves the first addition to 47bf71cc78d13c06e1eaa4d9842e6f94ddce4bea. git log -L over the added galaxy-result processing also traces those lines to that commit. git cat-file -p shows it is a normal one-parent commit, parent 66f278bb2be0e8183d56eede615d7cc370f38303, so no squash/member decomposition is needed.

The vulnerable mechanism is therefore absent from the direct parent.

Authorization/reachability: app/Controller/Component/ACLComponent.php grants eventTemplates/add and eventTemplates/edit to perm_template users; EventTemplatesController.php calls __setBuilderConfig() on GET add and GET edit. Thus a low-privileged authenticated template author can receive the leaked picker configuration; edit additionally enforces own-organisation ownership of the template, which does not constrain the separate Galaxy query.

The advisory-referenced d3adfe1a097dd4b403364e9af34e208660eeec1a is an incomplete attempted repair: it adds an OR condition containing 'Galaxy.distribution' > 0, which PHP evaluates before building the query rather than expressing a CakePHP field comparison. reasoning: The vulnerability is an authorization-category error, not a defect in RequireScopes itself: the middleware correctly checks the declared capability, but the PUT route declared a read capability for a credential-changing operation. The pre-existing UpdateUser password mutation becomes reachable to a restricted scoped token through that mapping, and login converts the changed credential into a session token that scopes intentionally do not constrain. Mainline history points to the large PR #195 squash, but the public PR member chain is reconstructable and isolates b47fa1c75d890cd080e3f6699bbfca8cd8d4b939 as the member that first wrote the flawed mapping. Its immediate parent tree lacks that mapping, while the final member tree equals the squash tree, so the aggregate is not treated as the BIC. The source remains flawed through v4.4.2 and direct fix 057e8b0b713d105eca7040ade810a057397613fa introduces and requires profile:write in v4.4.3. Because the smallest causal BIC itself carries the commit-object marker Made-with: Cursor, the appropriate closed verdict is AI_ROOT_CAUSE.

causal_chain.bug_semantics: The scoped-token rollout guarded the mutating PUT /user route with the read-only profile:read capability. RequireScopes therefore admitted an access token carrying only profile:read, while UpdateUser trusted the token's associated admin identity and allowed its password to be replaced. The token holder could then log in with the replacement password and receive a session JWT; session JWTs deliberately bypass scope checks, turning a read-only token into unrestricted administrator access.

GitHub later landed the PR as squash commit 3f8fb150158723aca31df2ae937a1aa7b31ac254, so the original member rather than the aggregate is the smallest BIC.

causal_chain.bug_semantics: An administrator or authenticated caller with connect-write authority can persist an attacker-chosen ConnectURL. The public GET /api/connects/info path, and later the authenticated connection-health path, cause the server to append /api/connect and issue an unrestricted outbound HTTP request to that stored URL. Because the request primitive performs no URL, resolved-address, redirect, loopback, private-network, or link-local/cloud-metadata validation, the caller can make the Ech0 server reach internal services and metadata endpoints and return or infer their responses.
causal_chain.flaw_origin: fabee479ccf98c081bb065926c726b461a42fdf3 first moved peer-detail retrieval from the browser into the server: it added publicRoutes.GET("/connects/info", controllers.GetConnectsInfo), GetConnectsInfo's iteration over stored ConnectURL values, and pkg.SendRequest implemented with an unconstrained http.Client.Do. The same commit therefore created both the server-side attacker-controlled request and the missing trust-boundary validation; later copies, retries, health checks, rewrites, and the fetchPeerConnectInfo extraction preserved rather than originated that mechanism.

Its cloudRestricted middleware validated an internal API key only when neither SELF_HOSTED nor DISABLE_ACCOUNT_PORTAL was set; in those self-hosted/account-portal-disabled modes it simply called next(). causal_chain.bug_semantics: An authenticated non-administrator can select a directory whose root path is allowed even though a descendant is denied by a path rule. Copy, rename, and delete then recurse over the filesystem subtree without authorizing each source descendant and, for copy/rename, the corresponding destination descendant. The user can therefore expose or relocate denied content at an allowed destination, or destroy it by deleting its allowed parent.

causal_chain.bug_semantics: Access rules treated the request path as a case-sensitive, slash-separated string and performed literal/prefix matching before the same path was resolved by the host filesystem. On case-insensitive filesystems, a case variant of a denied path therefore missed the rule but named the denied file; on Windows, backslashes and traversal components likewise missed the rule but were normalized by the filesystem. An authenticated user could consequently disclose or mutate an administrator-denied file within the user's filesystem scope.
causal_chain.flaw_origin: Commit 9c36dea485ddd16a90f0a615e20baddaee6b9cde first added the access-rule model and its vulnerable enforcement in one change: filemanager.go's User.Allowed compared the uncanonicalized URL with strings.HasPrefix(url, rule.Path), while newly added http.go passed raw request-derived paths to Allowed and then performed filesystem operations. Its immediate parent 780f1bc16e4e5270fed2a6b7da442a47084d8c4b contains none of Rule, User.Allowed, or that comparison. Later commits only moved, extracted, or broadened this mechanism, and the v2 rewrite aggregate preserved it.

causal_chain.bug_semantics: An authenticated BASIC app user can POST /api/attachments/:datasourceId/url. The route's TABLE/WRITE authorization is satisfied by the built-in BASIC role, and getSignedUploadURL loads the named S3 datasource, then uses its stored IAM credentials to presign a PutObject for the request body's bucket and key. Thus a non-builder can obtain an upload capability; where the datasource has no configured bucket constraint, the caller can select any bucket writable by those IAM credentials.
causal_chain.flaw_origin: The exploitable authorization regression begins in 23d75319026aec328a707e40e9437cb3bd6d9912, which replaced authorized(BUILDER) with authorized(PermissionType.TABLE, PermissionLevel.READ) on the signed-upload route. Commit 3e881e13186eb9da19c37deb2f55b3ab46e560b8 tightened READ to WRITE before release, but BASIC is the built-in WRITE role, so it retained the same unauthorized access. The controller's caller-controlled bucket sink pre-existed; 23d7531 is the smallest commit that exposed that sink to BASIC users.

causal_chain.bug_semantics: An authenticated user with Create permission could create a TUS upload with a small finite Upload-Length, then send a PATCH body larger than Upload-Length minus Upload-Offset. tusPatchHandler streamed the entire body to the file with io.Copy before comparing the resulting offset with the cached declared length; reaching or exceeding that length merely completed the upload. The excess bytes therefore remained on disk, and repeated oversized PATCH uploads could exhaust the filesystem.
causal_chain.flaw_origin: PR #5270 member 6337c4452529dfc018885a7d05cc4f1e217316c5 first made FileBrowser accept and retain the client's finite Upload-Length: it added registerUpload/getActiveUploadLength, retrieved that value in tusPatchHandler, and used it only after the pre-existing unbounded io.Copy to unregister a completed upload. Its direct parent advertised Upload-Length: -1 and neither parsed nor tracked a declared length, so the advisory-specific promise-and-bypass mechanism did not yet exist. GitHub later squash-merged the PR as 0f27c91eca581482ce4f82f6429f5dac12f8b64e.

POST /api/settings nevertheless accepted the ownership-establishing _set_password pseudo-setting: save_settings() hashed the attacker-chosen value into settings.json as password_hash, turning authentication on. A remote unauthenticated first caller could therefore choose the initial credential, authenticate (and, after the later session-continuity change, receive a session immediately), and lock out the intended operator. It added no locality, bootstrap token, or existing-owner check around that transition. A later commit only added automatic cookie issuance; it did not originate the takeover because an attacker could already log in with the password they selected.

causal_chain.bug_semantics: A logged-in user could submit a saved graph configuration whose config_json was checked only for syntactically valid JSON. The server stored and returned the object without a property allowlist; an administrator's list included every user's saved configurations. Loading one parsed the stored JSON and applyConfig spread every property of attacker-controlled stixStyles or mispStyles entries into GRAPH_CONFIG. Those style maps were then passed to Pivotick as nodeStyleMap/defaultNodeStyle, and Pivotick interpreted a supplied svgIcon as HTML, so viewing/loading the saved configuration could execute attacker script in another user's browser.
causal_chain.flaw_origin: Commit a0a9834b21b40ab570db54e1c6e6c2cf100b5f9a introduced the complete unsafe saved-configuration path in one focused feature commit: the graph_config model and save/list routes, unrestricted JSON persistence, the saved-config loader, and applyConfig's unrestricted style-object spreads. Its immediate parent had none of the graph-config persistence, loading, or patch-application mechanism, making this ordinary one-parent feature commit the smallest reconstructable BIC rather than the later branch merge or a release commit.

reasoning: The attack path begins when an operator connects cti-transmute to a remote MISP. The BIC's backend requests /events/index, parses the remote JSON, and returns selected fields essentially verbatim; the BIC's frontend then embeds those fields into HTML strings assigned to innerHTML. This directly enables a remote MISP controller to break out of text/attribute/style contexts in the event table, TLP warning, or flash surface. Exact-string history and line history identify b9f40af30de83fa44a14a3b0263df26192696b48, not a later rename/refactor or the May 20 feature expansion, as the first writer of the vulnerable event-row and related rendering mechanism. Its immediate parent 4637cf8255487759ba648cff7e374d7c995468a5 has neither the remote-MISP browser nor its rendering functions, so parent absence is directly verified. The one-parent BIC is an ordinary coherent feature commit, not a squash aggregate requiring member decomposition. The vulnerability persists into v1.3 and v1.4; direct fix 95e64137358d6fb7f1711523de2bf02ff6b181a7 DOM-builds remote fields with textContent and validates tag colors, and is contained by v1.5. Finally, attribution is based only on the BIC commit object: it has a human author/committer and no AI marker or trailer. Under the protocol, that makes the closed verdict NOT_AI regardless of AI signals on unrelated commits.

causal_chain.bug_semantics: Remote-data DOM XSS in the MISP event browser: the server accepts an operator-selected remote MISP instance, copies that instance's event fields into JSON, and the browser interpolates those values into template strings assigned to innerHTML. A malicious or compromised remote MISP can therefore inject markup or script-capable content through event IDs, information, organization/date/count/threat fields, tag names and colors, TLP/distribution labels, or flash/error text; unvalidated tag colors also enter inline CSS.
causal_chain.flaw_origin: Commit b9f40af30de83fa44a14a3b0263df26192696b48 added the remote-MISP connection/browser feature and, in the same atomic commit, passed remote response fields through website/web/convert/convert.py and rendered them with div.innerHTML, overlay.innerHTML, and tr.innerHTML in website/web/templates/convert/misp_to_stix.html. The core mistake was treating remote-derived strings and colors as trusted HTML/CSS instead of creating DOM nodes and assigning textContent plus validating colors. Commit 26ecb7e6a608b5be73fa552928e00bef7cac4f22 later expanded selection/distribution behavior and added further instances of the same mechanism, but b9f40af30de83fa44a14a3b0263df26192696b48 is the earliest and smallest real BIC for the vulnerable event-browser mechanism.

causal_chain.bug_semantics: rConfig deliberately disabled Laravel self-registration with Auth::routes(['register' => false]), but a later bare Auth::routes() call registered the framework's default registration endpoints again. An unauthenticated POST /register therefore reached RegisterController, whose create() method omitted role; the users.role database column defaulted to Admin, and the RegistersUsers flow authenticated the newly created account. The attacker consequently obtained a logged-in Administrator account without invitation, approval, or prior credentials.

The already-present disabled-registration call, framework registration controller, and Admin column default made that new route dangerous, but they did not expose registration while the only auth route declaration had register=false. The candidate's immediate parent 6202a5d9e061fce98de25ec8b62a4973c0dffd35 has no bare call.

A user able to set Kubernetes Node annotations can therefore feed untrusted content into a root-privileged shell-command path on every flannel node using this backend, enabling cross-node command injection; non-Extension backends do not execute this path.

causal_chain.bug_semantics: On Linux/Unix, LocalFolderExtractor first constructs and canonicalizes new File(destination, archiveEntryName) while backslashes in the untrusted RAR name are still literal filename characters. A name such as '..\..\tmp\evil' therefore passes the destination-prefix check. If the file does not exist, makeFile then splits that same name on backslashes and rejoins the components with File.separator, turning the previously literal '..' components into real '/' traversal. extract subsequently opens FileOutputStream on that reconstructed path and writes attacker-controlled archive content outside the extraction directory.
causal_chain.flaw_origin: The causal flaw is the two-stage, inconsistent interpretation of an archive pathname: validation and use do not operate on the same normalized representation. causal_chain.bug_semantics: Etherpad generated import/export working-file names in the shared process temporary directory from Math.random(), then used ordinary write, rename, and converter operations that follow existing symbolic links. A local low-privilege user who can predict a token and pre-create the corresponding /tmp path as a symlink can redirect Etherpad's file operation to a target writable by the Etherpad process, causing disclosure or overwrite; import output can contain attacker-influenced converted document content.
causal_chain.flaw_origin: The earliest causal origin is eeddf1348f351c92355d010ced56c3b511ca8f46: the initial document-export implementation created node/ExportHandler.js with Math.floor(Math.random()*new Date().getTime()), a hard-coded /tmp/eplite_export_ path, fs.writeFile(), and converter output at a sibling predictable path. b13fbbfd73ab18f69d45de382ffb1fc51fe96f1f added the same design to import two days later. Commits 4fc4a3538148bc995fff989794e91779ed4c847f and b0976a292f70c2c6d344bafd2793aed09027f74b later changed the token formula to Math.random()*0xFFFFFFFF, reducing it to the advisory's exact 32-bit form, but they did not originate the insecure shared-temp predictable-name mechanism.

Import acquired the same design in b13fbbf. The November 2011 0xFFFFFFFF edits made the current expression but inherited the same security defect, and subsequent directory/TypeScript changes are renames or migrations, so selecting any of them would mistake textual churn for causation. The flaw survived into v3.0.0 and was directly removed by 8c6104c5, which substitutes 128-bit crypto.randomBytes tokens in both handlers and is contained by v3.1.0. The smallest causal BIC is therefore the single-parent, non-squash eeddf134 commit. Its commit object has only the named human author/committer and no AI trailer or bot identity. Under the required BIC-only attribution rule, later AI involvement in discovery or remediation cannot attribute this 2011 introduction, so the closed verdict is NOT_AI.

Decomposing the 13-member branch shows that earlier members culminate at parent 229707951c66c6796a2ed6ca75872545df9a60c4 without operations.ts; cf80a02d23d99b0f4eebe4ac5eb42059f34b2b3d then creates the file, the permissive operation-key schemas, and the service path that consumes them. causal_chain.bug_semantics: An authenticated environment-key holder can supply a run-metadata operation whose unconstrained key is a JSONHero path such as $.__proto__.polluted. applyMetadataOperations passes that key to JSONHeroPath.set on a normal cloned object without rejecting __proto__, constructor, or prototype segments, so the write reaches Object.prototype in the shared webapp process; inherited attacker properties then corrupt unrelated Prisma and metrics objects across tenants and can crash the process.
causal_chain.flaw_origin: PR #1563 added the metadata-operations API and, in its member commit cf80a02d23d99b0f4eebe4ac5eb42059f34b2b3d, created packages/core/src/v3/runMetadata/operations.ts with JSONHeroPath(operation.key).set(...) while simultaneously defining every keyed operation schema with key: z.string(). The endpoint's API-key-authenticated request body was therefore connected directly to a prototype-walking setter with no dangerous-segment validation from the feature's first implementation.

reasoning: The vulnerability is a trust-boundary failure, not merely the existence of EL: gadget.jsf turns a request parameter into an arbitrary gadget XML location, then places parsed gadget content into a JSFT/JSF rendering context where EL is evaluated and output escaping is disabled. Commit 16e12748 supplied loader primitives, but no external request path; ece6ab82 is the first minimal commit completing the exploit chain by adding gadget.jsf, so later copyright edits, workspace moves, the 2018 Eclipse initial import, and dependency upgrades are not introducers. Direct inspection of the immediate parent tree proves gadget.jsf absent. The historical endpoint survives the Eclipse import and is present at the 7.0.0 affected boundary. The 2026 remediation restricts dangerous EL resolution in jsftemplating and GlassFish consumes it at 7.0.26, 7.1.1, and 8.0.2. Only the ece6ab82 commit object was used for AI attribution; its human 2009 identity and trailer-free message provide no AI marker, so the closed verdict is NOT_AI.

causal_chain.bug_semantics: The Admin Console gadget bootstrap accepts the request-controlled gadget parameter as a URL/path, parses the referenced XML into a GadgetModule, and emits the module text with escaping disabled inside JSFTemplating. That template path evaluates EL in the attacker-controlled XML/content (the source itself warns that JSFT content is evaluated twice), so expressions such as #{7*7} execute server-side and richer EL access to constructors, static methods/fields, getClass(), or class can reach arbitrary code execution.
causal_chain.flaw_origin: The causal origin is the 2009 gadget endpoint commit ece6ab82e495d2cf87cbf4ec78170727adf2c7f1: it first added gadget.jsf and wired #{param.gadget} into gf.getGadgetModule while rendering pageSession.gadget.text through escape=false. The immediately preceding infrastructure commit 16e12748c3def5754a21f3019a1794b899862017 supplied the URL-capable XML loader, but had no request-reachable gadget.jsf endpoint; ece6ab82 is therefore the smallest commit that completed the vulnerable untrusted-input-to-EL-evaluation path.

audit_record.flaw_origin: The original member commit for PR #194 introduced the rating input model and renderer together: packages/models/src/features/blocks/inputs/rating.ts accepted customIcon.svg with z.string().optional(), while packages/js/src/features/blocks/inputs/rating/components/RatingForm.tsx selected props.customIcon.svg and passed it directly to innerHTML without sanitization. This is the first public commit object that wrote the flawed data-to-DOM mechanism; later moves, formatting changes, and accessibility refactors preserved it.

reasoning: The vulnerability is a stored-XSS lifecycle, not merely the final PlateBlock spelling. Authoring already allowed rich-text links, and the v2 JavaScript viewer first exposed the unsafe stored data in 3487850 by injecting serialized HTML without scheme validation. That exact member commit is smaller and causally prior to the recreated mainline PR carrier. e0a9824 removed redundant html/plainText storage and rewrote rendering to use richText nodes, but its direct href retained the same trust-boundary failure; 765c4b2 later retained it again. Therefore neither refactor is the BIC. Direct inspection of 3487850's parent tree proves the new viewer sink absent, while tree identity with 1a3869 proves how the decomposed member landed. The landed tree precedes the first js-v0.0.1 tag and remains vulnerable through js-v0.10.0. Fix 2c3fc7 applies protocol allowlisting, is exactly js-v0.10.1, and is included in v3.16.0 but not v3.15.2. Finally, attribution is based only on the decomposed BIC commit object: it is authored and committed by Baptiste Arnaud and contains no AI marker. Any AI signal on the later fix cannot attribute the 2022 root cause, so the closed verdict is NOT_AI.

causal_chain.bug_semantics: An authenticated bot author can store a rich-text link whose URL uses the javascript: scheme. The @typebot.io/js viewer rendered that author-controlled link into the DOM without validating its scheme—initially by assigning serialized content.html to SolidJS innerHTML and, after a 2023 refactor, by assigning the rich-text element URL directly to an anchor href. When a visitor clicks the link, the browser executes the payload in the embedding host page's origin, allowing theft of host-origin cookies, session tokens, and other accessible data; victim authentication is not required.
causal_chain.flaw_origin: The smallest reconstructable BIC is PR #194's sole member commit 3487850b9f4808617d347ddde4d9701f56662894. It created packages/js/src/features/blocks/bubbles/textBubble/components/TextBubble.tsx and introduced the unsafe sink innerHTML={props.content.html} for author-controlled serialized rich text, while the pre-existing builder toolbar already exposed LinkToolbarButton without a protocol allowlist. GitHub landed the same parent and identical tree as mainline carrier 1a3869ae6d9fa92fc71ef9d981bfffb8e4ee4ecc. Commit e0a9824913237cb5340d262770e9e8290fbc4002 later replaced the stored-HTML sink with a recursive Plate renderer containing <a href={props.element.url as string}>, preserving rather than originating the missing-scheme-validation flaw; 765c4b2f8c1fd4ec610bc81b2547efbda65452ae was another refactor of that same unsafe href.

reasoning: The vulnerability is not merely that the endpoint could make an outbound request; its defining flaw is the split security transaction introduced when a DNS-resolving SSRF check was added without binding its result to the eventual socket. The decomposed PR history is necessary because public commit d549137791f10c59c00ec3e89cb55cd560a8248f aggregates unrelated OAuth, authentication-timing, SSRF, and test work. Original member d34f611030166bbdd4ea2d93d909098c9dc8d934 is the smallest causal change: it alone adds the gateway-test validation call and then continues to pass the hostname URL to ResilientHttpClient. Its immediate parent f1c78d290e2901b4c58ee64e575e049b0f8b2bb3 has an unrestricted hostname request but not the advisory's check/use DNS race, so the exact vulnerable mechanism is absent there. Later commits 2b5b9e9a145304c466966c560e82d4682849b13a and fb4d9a2616f22dcc64239b250b1c6389b638de4f strengthened allowlisting and documented the known rebinding limitation; they preserved rather than originated the race. Direct fix fba11a99babd80779fa05510b35fb6a153bbacaf carries the checked IP into the actual request while preserving Host and TLS SNI, and its tag ancestry exactly matches the 1.0.3 patched boundary. Finally, the complete d34f611030166bbdd4ea2d93d909098c9dc8d934 commit object has human identities and no AI authorship marker, so under BIC-only attribution this is a closed NOT_AI result.

causal_chain.bug_semantics: The privileged /admin/gateways/test flow performed a security decision on DNS answers obtained while validating the submitted hostname, then gave an httpx-based ResilientHttpClient a URL containing that same hostname. The client therefore performed an independent connection-time resolution. An attacker controlling DNS could return a public address for validation and then rebind the hostname to a private, loopback, link-local, or cloud-metadata address for the actual request, bypassing the SSRF network checks.

SecurityValidator._validate_ssrf used socket.getaddrinfo for the check, but the member did not preserve or bind the checked address for the later connection. The repository landed PR #3115 as squash d549137791f10c59c00ec3e89cb55cd560a8248f; later allowlist work made the limitation more explicit but did not originate it.

causal_chain.bug_semantics: The unauthenticated static-download route passes request.getParameter("version") into BaseUtils.replaceFileNameAndExtension without validating it. For a request to the route base (/file/static/noauth in the renamed endpoint, formerly /downloadFile/static/noauth), the path-derived fileName is "noauth", whose full-path component is empty, so the helper replaces it entirely with attacker-controlled version. A value such as ../../etc/passwd is then handed to FileUtils.readFile(APP_DOWNLOAD_FOLDER_PATH, fileName, ...), which constructs new File(APP_DOWNLOAD_FOLDER_PATH, fileName) and can escape the intended download directory, exposing arbitrary readable files without authentication.
causal_chain.flaw_origin: Commit b34987f7b37b5fd6a03b9dd9092bd18efc936d46 added version as a cache/content-identity filename override during a resources/web-client refactor. The normal producer generated an ID for version, but DownloadFileRequestHandler treated the HTTP parameter as if it were trusted and reused it as a filesystem child path. The already-existing security rule exempted /downloadFile/static/noauth/** from authentication, making this new trust-boundary error remotely reachable immediately.

causal_chain.bug_semantics: ZPan initialized its process-wide HS512 JWT helper with the public constant "123". A remote attacker who knows that repository-visible secret can sign a z-token whose subject and roles claim an administrator identity; LoginAuthWithRoles accepts the signature and then authorizes protected API routes from the attacker-controlled roles, bypassing password authentication.
causal_chain.flaw_origin: Commit 4fae6e2bdcab183ef59dd9f4055e2633ec2523f5 added the new user/token authentication subsystem. Its newly created internal/app/service/token.go made NewToken call jwtutil.Init("123") and used that same global helper to issue and verify RoleClaims; the same commit added the cookie-to-roles authentication middleware and protected-route role checks. The hard-coded signing key, rather than a per-installation secret, is therefore part of the original implementation of this authentication mechanism, not a later move or refactor of pre-existing vulnerable lines.

causal_chain.bug_semantics: An authenticated Project Manager or Owner can store a repository git_url beginning with Git's --upload-pack= option. The server-side schedule commit-hash poller passes that value directly after `git ls-remote` without an end-of-options delimiter; Git parses it as an option and invokes the attacker-selected upload-pack command through a shell, yielding command execution in the Semaphore server process.
causal_chain.flaw_origin: Commit a30df1527e15c4c0060979bc2b7b120a8234111f changed GetLastRemoteCommitHash from running `git ls-remote origin <branch>` in the already-cloned repository to running `git ls-remote <Repository.GetGitURL()> <branch>` in the temporary directory. That single-line data-flow change first placed the stored, attacker-controlled GitURL in Git's option-parsing position; the existing makeCmd helper appended the arguments to exec.Command("git") without `--`.

causal_chain.bug_semantics: A client can issue XKB SetMap requests with XkbSetMapResizeTypes so that CheckKeyTypes() computes nMaps from the client-controlled sum firstType + nTypes but checks only a lower bound. After growing num_types to 255, a request with firstType=255 and nTypes=10 passes the firstType > num_types test because equality is allowed, computes nMaps=265, and writes mapWidthRtrn[i + firstType] for indices 255 through 264. The caller supplies the fixed 256-byte stack array mapWidths[XkbMaxLegalKeyCode + 1], so indices 256 through 264 overwrite nine bytes beyond it into adjacent stack state, permitting denial of service and potentially privilege escalation when the X server runs privileged.
causal_chain.flaw_origin: The repository's initial X.Org R6.6 baseline commit ded6147bfb5d75ff1e67c858040a628b61bc17d1 added xkb/xkb.c with the complete vulnerable composition: a fixed XkbMaxLegalKeyCode+1 mapWidths stack buffer, client-controlled nMaps = firstType + nTypes with no upper bound, and the mapWidthRtrn[i + req->firstType] write. Whitespace/style changes and the 2010 zero-initialization of the same fixed-size array did not originate the mechanism.

causal_chain.bug_semantics: A remote caller could supply an arbitrary HTTP(S) target in GET /api's url query parameter. PullMD passed that value to its server-side web extractor and returned the fetched content without rejecting loopback, private, link-local, CGNAT, or cloud-metadata destinations or revalidating redirect targets, so a request such as /api?url=http://100.100.100.200/latest/user-data could disclose cloud instance metadata and reach other internal services.
causal_chain.flaw_origin: The root release commit wired req.query.url directly from server.js into extractWebFn(url), while lib/web.js wrapped globalThis.fetch only with a timeout and then called fetchFn(url, { headers }). It added no URL-scheme, hostname, DNS-result, IP-range, or redirect-hop policy between attacker input and the outbound request; that unsafe fetch design, rather than a later refactor or move, is the causal origin.

causal_chain.bug_semantics: An unauthenticated proxy client can put an arbitrary HTTP(S) origin in x-headroom-base-url. Headroom uses that origin as the upstream without establishing that its resolved addresses are public, forwards the incoming request headers and body to it, and returns the upstream response. A caller can therefore reach loopback, link-local/cloud-metadata, RFC 1918, and other internal services through the proxy and read their responses; the incoming Authorization header also follows the caller-selected destination. The reference compose deployment amplified reachability by publishing the proxy on 0.0.0.0 without requiring HEADROOM_PROXY_TOKEN.
causal_chain.flaw_origin: Commit 729cc035a474b4ff04c6c16c62d3a5f4e515c56f introduced the trust-boundary violation in headroom/proxy/server.py: the catch-all route read x-headroom-base-url and immediately passed custom_base.rstrip('/') to the pre-existing handle_passthrough method. That method copied all request headers except Host into the outbound request and relayed the response content/status/headers. The commit added no scheme, hostname, address-class, DNS, or operator-allowlist validation. Later commits moved the same catch-all mechanism and expanded it to dedicated OpenAI handlers; they did not originate the already exploitable SSRF.

reasoning: The vulnerability is not merely the older use of per-glyph metrics: the disclosed CWE-122 occurs when a maxbounds-sized CPU heap atlas is populated with unchecked per-glyph-sized copies. History shows the smallest commit that first created that exact allocation/copy mismatch is 732e3b9c08532f40656010eac9d128601cc88c3f; its parent used direct GL uploads and therefore lacked the heap buffer and heap memcpy sink. Later layout changes preserved the mismatch, and the 2026 fix added the missing dimensional invariant checks. causal_chain.bug_semantics: On a glamor-backed X server, glamor_font_get() sized a CPU-side font-atlas heap buffer and each glyph slot from the font's declared maxbounds, but copied each bitmap using that glyph's unchecked GLYPHWIDTHBYTES and GLYPHHEIGHTPIXELS metrics. libXfont2's PCF parser did not recompute maxbounds from the per-glyph records, so an authenticated X client could supply a PCF whose individual metrics exceeded (or were negative relative to) maxbounds; drawing text then made the row memcpy write attacker-controlled bytes beyond the allocated atlas, with negative values also permitting unsigned/size_t wrap.
causal_chain.flaw_origin: Commit 732e3b9c08532f40656010eac9d128601cc88c3f changed glamor_font_get() from issuing one glTexSubImage2D call per glyph to building one CPU heap staging atlas. It introduced bits = malloc(overall_width * overall_height), where overall_width/height came from maxbounds, together with a loop bounded by GLYPHHEIGHTPIXELS(glyph) and memcpy(dst, src, GLYPHWIDTHBYTES(glyph)) without checking those per-glyph dimensions against the maxbounds-derived slot. That new mismatch is the exact heap-buffer-overflow mechanism.

reasoning: The vulnerability is a composed trust-boundary failure, not merely the existence of a shell API. With webhook.enabled true, the BIC binds the webhook listener to every interface; an omitted token causes authenticate to approve every caller; handleHook accepts a caller-provided exec action; and executeShell supplies that string as the shell program. A usable request also needs a session key whose platform context can be reconstructed, and possibly a project selector, but neither substitutes for authentication. The 6ae088a commit introduced all of these pieces at once and even added a test requiring empty-token authentication to pass. Its immediate parent has no core/webhook.go or equivalent webhook-exec route, so absence is tree-proven. Pickaxe history finds no earlier writer, while the only later sink change is a behavior-preserving helper refactor. Tag membership brackets introduction between v1.2.2-beta.1 and v1.2.2-beta.2 and confirms persistence through the advisory's v1.4.1 boundary. There is no remediation commit: both the latest stable tag and audited HEAD retain the bypass and shell dispatch, so null fix fields are justified and unpatched status is recorded. Finally, the smallest BIC's own commit object explicitly says `generated by llmgit` and credits Claude as co-author. Since that AI-marked object is the first writer of the flawed authentication-plus-exec design, the causal verdict is AI_ROOT_CAUSE.

causal_chain.bug_semantics: When the optional webhook server is enabled, it listens on all interfaces and accepts POST requests containing an attacker-controlled exec string. Authentication is fail-open: WebhookServer.authenticate returns true whenever the configured token is empty, a state the configuration comments explicitly describe as 'empty = no auth'. The handler then dispatches req.Exec to a shell with -c/-Command. Thus an attacker who supplies a nonempty, reconstructable session_key (and a project when multiple projects are configured) can execute an arbitrary shell program as the cc-connect process without a credential. The shell interpretation of exec is an intentional feature; the security failure is exposing that full shell capability across a network endpoint while treating an omitted token as authorization.
causal_chain.flaw_origin: The complete vulnerable mechanism originated in the single-parent feature commit 6ae088a658077a2f11a83ded6ac53c0dbddefd38: it created core/webhook.go, added the network listener and /hook handler, defined the JSON exec field, made an empty token authenticate successfully, passed exec to sh -c, wired the server into main, and documented an empty token as disabling authentication. This is the smallest repository-visible BIC, not the later shell-helper refactor.

evidence: First-party report https://github.com/chenhg5/cc-connect/issues/1488 identifies core/webhook.go's empty-token authentication bypass, exec dispatch, all-interface listener, and shell sink; maintainer @chenhg5 replied on 2026-07-03 that the report was confirmed valid and described the same two-part chain. Source review adds an important reachability qualification: handleHook requires a nonempty session_key, resolveEngine must succeed, and executeShell must reconstruct the named platform context. Consequently, the issue's displayed curl body, which omits session_key, would be rejected at the required-field check, but adding a valid/reconstructable session key reaches the confirmed unauthenticated shell path.

`git show 6ae088a658077a2f11a83ded6ac53c0dbddefd38 -- core/webhook.go config/config.go config.example.toml cmd/cc-connect/main.go` shows one cohesive +503-line webhook feature. In core/webhook.go it creates WebhookRequest.Exec, starts http.Server at fmt.Sprintf(":%d", ws.port), routes POST /hook through authenticate, returns true for ws.token == "", dispatches req.Exec, and runs exec.CommandContext(ctx, "sh", "-c", req.Exec). config/config.go and config.example.toml state that an empty token means no authentication, while main.go starts the listener whenever webhook.enabled is true.

The BIC's newly added core/webhook_test.go makes the insecure policy explicit: TestWebhookServer_NoTokenRequired creates a server with an empty token and asserts authenticate succeeds. The same test file validates that exec is accepted as one of the two request action types, corroborating that no-token access and network-triggered exec were deliberately shipped together rather than accidentally joined by later history.

History searches `git log --all -S 'if ws.token == ""' -- core/webhook.go` and `git log --all -S 'req.Exec' -- core/webhook.go` each identify 6ae088a658077a2f11a83ded6ac53c0dbddefd38 as the first writer. The complete path log contains only the introducer, a later broad error-handling commit b9af7ea7ba641eb9278d45c9a19f361692acef44, and shell-configuration refactor 6feaf90f2f8cccec2203169b4d0edc3edd538837. The latter only replaces direct sh -c construction with shellExecCommand while continuing to pass req.Exec, so it preserves rather than introduces the vulnerable trust boundary.

Immediate-parent verification is direct: `git ls-tree -r --name-only 805045501b12fd3cf3834d19b0b882b32803e8c2 -- core/webhook.go` returns no path, and `git diff-tree --name-status 805045501b12fd3cf3834d19b0b882b32803e8c2 6ae088a658077a2f11a83ded6ac53c0dbddefd38 -- core/webhook.go` reports `A core/webhook.go`. Therefore the parent tree lacks the endpoint, empty-token bypass, request exec field, and webhook shell sink. The BIC is a one-parent public-DAG feature commit; no smaller reachable member commits exist to decompose.

Release-boundary check: v1.2.2-beta.1 resolves to ecea1ef36d86bb70dd633fb342f655d108ea52cb (2026-03-12) and lacks core/webhook.go, while the 2026-03-14 BIC is contained by v1.2.2-beta.2, which resolves to 9223201696e3f91b2f9fb456bba7dcef0a76bcd3 (2026-03-16). `git tag --contains 6ae088a...` starts at v1.2.2-beta.2 and includes v1.4.1. Direct `git grep` confirms both `if ws.token == ""` and the req.Exec shell sink in v1.2.2-beta.2 and v1.4.1; v1.2.2-beta.1 has neither. This places the introduction before the affected upper-bound release named by the advisory.

No fix is present in the validated public history. `git log --all -- core/webhook.go` has no post-6feaf90 remediation, `git log --all -S 'if ws.token == ""'` has no removal, and direct tag-tree checks show the bypass plus req.Exec-to-shell path still present in stable v1.5.0 (17c61062c2f9ce9bcdd45a2082e491f9743a2770, 2026-08-16) and HEAD/v1.5.1-beta.1 (80713167d17b3f2a3906efc3b14b3acab39766e4, 2026-08-28). causal_chain.bug_semantics: For a window drawable, do_get_buffers allocated only count + 1 DRI2BufferPtr slots, filled count client-requested slots, and then used arithmetic attachment counters to decide whether to append implicit front buffers. With at least two DRI2BufferBackLeft requests and one DRI2BufferFrontLeft request, need_real_front remained positive even though FrontLeft was already present, so a redundant real-front pointer was appended at buffers[count]. The FrontLeft request also made need_fake_front positive, so the fake-front pointer was then written at buffers[count + 1], one pointer beyond the heap allocation. The DRI2GetBuffers and DRI2GetBuffersWithFormat request paths both called this helper, allowing a local X client to crash the server or potentially escalate privileges when it ran as root.
causal_chain.flaw_origin: Commit ff6c7764c2909e4126403b7211faa6c58556b341 replaced the parent's bulk CreateBuffers path with per-attachment allocation and introduced need_real_front++/-- alongside the existing fake-front accounting, while retaining an allocation sized for only one implicit attachment. The parent could append at most one fake front and therefore respected its count + 1 capacity; the new combination could append both a redundant real front and a fake front. Treating attachment presence as signed counts rather than boolean presence broke the allocation invariant.

causal_chain.bug_semantics: With federation enabled, NodeBB authenticated the HTTP-signature key against the ActivityPub activity actor and required object.id to have that actor's origin, but did not bind object.attributedTo to the authenticated actor. A remote actor could therefore send a signed Create whose object.id was on the attacker's origin but whose attributedTo was a bare local numeric uid such as 1. The inbound mock copied attributedTo into the post/message uid; actors.assert filtered numeric identifiers out and its false result was ignored, after which topic or chat persistence treated the attacker-chosen local uid as the author.
causal_chain.flaw_origin: Commit f74775365a57262488434c920c7b805608b761c7 first made the unsafe attribution mapping remotely exploitable: it added inbox.create, took only req.body.object for authorship, passed the untrusted object through activitypub.mocks.post, and persisted the resulting postData without comparing attributedTo to the authenticated req.body.actor. The unsafe mocks.post assignment had been prepared in f1e5e5a0ad4cc6d5a02bf9bc952e524fe2f58458 and moved by 06e1583461f034d68c8c3c6d69547b06ad6ab3b5, but f74775365a57262488434c920c7b805608b761c7 is the smallest commit that connected it to the inbound Create attack surface and made the remote post-forgery path real.

causal_chain.bug_semantics: During ListFonts/ListFontsWithInfo alias resolution, libXfont2 can return a fonts.alias target up to MAXFONTNAMELEN (1024) bytes, but the server used 256-byte tmp_pattern and LFWIstateRec.pattern buffers and copied resolvedlen/namelen bytes into them without first checking either length. A local client able to add a crafted font directory with SetFontPath and request the alias can therefore drive a 257-1023 byte target through the font provider and overflow stack-resident state, causing a crash or potentially privilege escalation when the server is privileged.
causal_chain.flaw_origin: The first xserver repository commit containing the mechanism, the R6.6 baseline import, simultaneously added #define XLFDMAXFONTNAMELEN 256 in include/closestr.h and the unchecked memmove(tmp_pattern, resolved, resolvedlen) and memmove(c->current.pattern, name, namelen) alias paths in dix/dixfonts.c. Its immediate parent contains neither file. Later formatting, memmove-to-memcpy, and libXfont2 API migration commits preserved rather than originated the size mismatch and unchecked length-controlled writes.

causal_chain.bug_semantics: A remote Bluetooth device can supply an EIR name element whose field_len is 254, making eir_parse pass data_len 253 to name2utf8. On the non-UTF-8 conversion path, name2utf8 used strncpy with that attacker-controlled length to copy into utf8_name[HCI_MAX_NAME_LENGTH + 2]. HCI_MAX_NAME_LENGTH is 248, so the 250-byte stack array is overrun by three bytes; the missing terminator can also make the subsequent stripping and duplication read beyond the array. Discovery therefore permits a radio-adjacent unauthenticated peer to crash bluetoothd and potentially corrupt control data.
causal_chain.flaw_origin: Commit 155fa21473ada6d3e7773175186badd4bc0fde22 first added src/eir.c:name2utf8 and coupled the fixed 250-byte utf8_name array to strncpy(..., len), where len is derived from the untrusted EIR element length and can be 253. Although the subject calls the change a move, the removed src/event.c code copied at the fixed MGMT_MAX_NAME_LENGTH bound, while the newly added EIR helper introduced the attacker-length copy; it is therefore the smallest causal introducer rather than a pure move. Later commit 218db700f49370bc07ce1e6d609d28d846470d99 changed character conversion but retained the already-vulnerable array and copy.

Its direct parent lacks the entire file, while both origin-tracing methods identify c2681402 as the first writer of the decisive fail-open check and remote-to-shell assignment. The first vulnerable tagged boundary is v1.2.2-beta.2 and the mechanism persists through v1.4.1, v1.5.0, and the audited HEAD, so there is no fix SHA to record. causal_chain.bug_semantics: When the opt-in Management API is enabled with its token left empty, its authentication middleware treats the empty secret as successful authentication. The server listens on all interfaces at port 9820, and an unauthenticated remote POST to /api/v1/cron can copy attacker-controlled JSON exec text into a persisted CronJob. The cron scheduler identifies a nonempty Exec as a shell job and ultimately runs that text through the configured shell, so the attacker obtains command execution when the job fires; later code also added an immediate /api/v1/cron/{id}/exec trigger, but that was not necessary for the original scheduled-execution path.
causal_chain.flaw_origin: The vulnerable trust-boundary crossing was created in one change: c2681402a7686294174a263e31245a52d4fea380 added the network-facing Management API, deliberately made authenticate return true for an empty token, registered the cron endpoints behind that fail-open middleware, and assigned untrusted req.Exec directly to CronJob.Exec. The shell-capable CronJob and its sh -c execution sink already existed in the parent; c2681402 is the smallest commit that made that sink reachable from an unauthenticated remote management request.

reasoning: The original Layer C hole feature cached fragments, but before f066a8838e49ba211250c56c2955a25689e5e7ca the endpoint had no attacker-controlled originating-page URL and did not derive route-sensitive output from u. The BIC made u influence the rendered route path/slug and source request while varying the shared key only by u's query. Two requests whose u values have different pathnames but the same inner query therefore collide; the first unauthenticated request populates the process-wide entry and subsequent legitimate visitors receive its route-dependent body until invalidation or eviction. Both the tainted render input and the incomplete cache key first appear together in this single non-merge commit, so no squash decomposition is needed, and the immediate parent directly proves the mechanism absent. The BIC predates and belongs to every tagged release, satisfying the lower affected boundary, but public history disproves a patch at 0.0.15: later tags and main retain the vulnerable lines, so no real fix SHA can be supplied. Under the BIC-only attribution rule, the human author/committer and complete absence of AI trailers or bot identity require NOT_AI.

causal_chain.bug_semantics: The unauthenticated GET /_instatic/hole/<nodeId> handler treats the attacker-controlled u parameter as the originating page URL and uses its path, slug, and query to render a shared hole, but its process-wide cache key contains only nodeId, publish version, and u's normalized inner query. Because u's pathname is content-varying but absent from the key, an attacker can render route-dependent HTML for a chosen pathname into the slot later used by a legitimate request with the same nodeId, version, and query.
causal_chain.flaw_origin: Commit f066a8838e49ba211250c56c2955a25689e5e7ca first forwarded location.pathname + location.search as u, parsed u into pageUrl, exposed pageUrl-derived route.path and route.slug to rendering and request-dependent loop sources, and simultaneously keyed shared-hole responses as v=<version>&normalizeQuery(pageUrl.searchParams), omitting the content-varying pageUrl pathname. The older hole cache existed, but its parent did not accept u or render from an attacker-selected page URL, so it did not contain this poisoning mechanism.

The security branch directly fixes WEB-02 in ac962fcce374739572c04e09269c12b9daeb457f, and the landed fix 1f96dabc19130947770353cd6e814db4fd96e6a0 centralizes identity resolution so a network caller cannot choose another partition. causal_chain.bug_semantics: When proxy memory is enabled, the proxy treats the caller-controlled x-headroom-user-id header as the authoritative memory partition key without authenticating or otherwise binding that value to the caller. A remote client can select a victim identifier, causing memory search results to be injected into the attacker's LLM context and memory tool operations to read, create, update, or delete records in the victim's partition; this is a CWE-639 confidentiality and integrity failure.
causal_chain.flaw_origin: Commit da743418584725e8b9c3315dc1aea7cf5e949192 first integrated persistent memory into the network proxy and wrote memory_user_id = headers.get("x-headroom-user-id") in headroom/proxy/server.py, then passed that untrusted value directly to search_and_format_context and handle_memory_tool_calls. The pre-existing reference docker-compose configuration already bound the proxy to 0.0.0.0 and published port 8787, and the BIC added no caller authentication or identity binding, so the new partition selector was remotely attacker-controlled in the shipped deployment model.

reasoning: CVE-2026-77806 is the regression/variant created while SPIP was changing header extraction for 4.4.20, not the later Metasploit exploit implementation referenced by the advisory. The smallest causal change is d369f5a49c3593f18b1c81fc3a3051bd0bed1e1d: it introduced the exact combination that matters, extraction of each PHP block's inner text plus ^/$ anchors interpreted per-line because of /m. The immediate parent directly lacks that combination, while 4.4.20 contains it. Commit 36b9847a7c14e5a069425d7d3104d22ccfecc680 removes only m, precisely closing the injection primitive, and is contained in fixed release 4.4.21 but not vulnerable 4.4.20. The BIC is a normal direct source commit and needs no squash decomposition. causal_chain.bug_semantics: In SPIP 4.4.20, analyse_resultat_skel() examined the inner text of each PHP block with an anchored header() regular expression that mistakenly retained PCRE's multiline modifier. Because ^ and $ therefore matched individual lines rather than the whole PHP block, an unauthenticated attacker could inject a newline-delimited header("X-Spip-Filtre: intval|_request|system") line into generated template code. SPIP extracted that attacker-selected filter chain, intval reduced the body to the key 0, _request read attacker-controlled POST parameter 0, and system executed it, yielding pre-authentication remote code execution.
causal_chain.flaw_origin: The vulnerable product code is in the upstream spip/ecrire repository, not in the bundled rapid7/metasploit-framework reference. Commit d369f5a49c3593f18b1c81fc3a3051bd0bed1e1d rewrote public/composer.php to collect individual PHP blocks and first added the vulnerable /^...$/ims match over each block's innerHtml. Its immediate parent used a materially different whole-page preg_match_all implementation and did not contain this vulnerable collector-plus-multiline-anchors mechanism. Rapid7 commit b16eca819abb8f1401f21d115e71e3dfc67b847c only added an exploit module and documentation after the SPIP flaw existed; it neither introduced nor fixed SPIP.

causal_chain.bug_semantics: With OAuth enabled behind a TLS-terminating reverse proxy, Temporal UI Server created browser authentication cookies with Secure set from c.Request().TLS, which describes only the proxy-to-server hop. When that hop was HTTP, the access-token user cookies (and later refresh-token cookies when an IdP issued one) lacked Secure even though the browser used HTTPS. causal_chain.bug_semantics: A template-controlled reverse range such as (100000000..1) makes evalRangeToken charge high - low + 1, a large negative count. Limiter.use accepted that negative count and added it to its cumulative base, creating artificial budget credit. Later append/replace operations could therefore exceed the configured memoryLimit; flattening the resulting large V8 cons-string could terminate the Node.js process, producing denial of service.
causal_chain.flaw_origin: Commit 2af297f81ac465feb3277ba7b92f7236409370b0 added ctx.memoryLimit.use(high - low + 1) to src/render/expression.ts without constraining the charge to a non-negative range size. The pre-existing Limiter.use implementation accepted and accumulated signed counts, so this new attacker-controlled negative callsite completed the underflow/budget-bypass mechanism. Reverse ranges themselves return an empty array because range(start, stop) loops only while start < stop, making the negative charge pure budget credit rather than a matching allocation.

causal_chain.bug_semantics: The default-registered strip_html filter applied one global regular expression containing unbounded lazy script, style, comment, and generic-tag alternatives directly to attacker-controlled template data. On many opener tokens without a matching closer, V8 retries an alternative at each '<' and scans the remaining suffix looking for the absent terminator, producing quadratic work on the single Node.js event-loop thread. memoryLimit did not bound that CPU work because it charged only the input string length before String.replace ran.
causal_chain.flaw_origin: Commit 8e9e10fdb4c7f00ffa3997d3e2c0a0bfa48ce887 replaced the prior simple tag regex in filters.js with the Ruby-Liquid-compatible /<script.*?<\/script>|<!--.*?-->|<style.*?<\/style>|<.*?>/g expression. That functional-parity change first introduced the unbounded lazy alternatives and therefore the vulnerable repeated-suffix search; later moves and expansions preserved or broadened the same mechanism rather than originating it.

causal_chain.bug_semantics: LiquidJS treated a lexically resolved pathname under a configured template root as proof that the file ultimately opened was under that root. Node's file APIs then followed symlinks, so an attacker-controlled symlink located inside a trusted partials/layouts/root directory could target any readable file outside the directory; include, render, or layout would parse and render the external target.
causal_chain.flaw_origin: Commit 8fbbec089fa4e3db4bec47462b1c08dd65c36648 first introduced filesystem-backed template loading and the include tag. Its index.js handleCache() resolved the requested name with path.resolve(this.options.root, filepath) and immediately passed that non-canonical pathname to fs.readFileSync(), while tags/include.js routed an evaluated include name into handleCache(). That is the first complete path-check/path-construction-to-file-open mechanism that follows an in-root symlink without validating the target; later Loader.withinDir(), FS.contains(), file moves, and separate partials/layouts roots preserved or re-expressed the same flaw rather than introducing it.

causal_chain.bug_semantics: LiquidJS strip_html treated its output as tag-stripped text, but the generic-tag alternative <.*?> used JavaScript dot without dotAll, so it could not consume CR or LF inside angle brackets. Browsers accept those line terminators as whitespace between a tag name and attributes; consequently an attacker-controlled value such as <img\nsrc=x\nonerror=alert(1)> survived strip_html and became executable HTML/XSS when rendered without a separate escaping step.
causal_chain.flaw_origin: Commit 8e9e10fdb4c7f00ffa3997d3e2c0a0bfa48ce887 replaced the older tag-name-only strip_html regex in filters.js with a Ruby-Liquid-style alternation whose new generic branch was <.*?>. That one-line change first wrote the exact vulnerable construct: JavaScript '.' stops at CR/LF while browsers continue parsing the tag. Later moves and refactors preserved it. Commit 42d25902e855d3c06d5ead071bf55604f495c205 made script, style, and comment alternatives multiline-safe with [\s\S] but retained <.*?>; it sharpened the inconsistency described by the advisory but is not the BIC because the flawed generic branch already existed in its parent.

causal_chain.bug_semantics: Preact distinguishes genuine VNodes by giving them an own constructor value of undefined. In the affected client renderer, the gate became `if (newVNode.constructor != UNDEFINED) return NULL`; JavaScript loose equality treats null and undefined as equal, so a JSON-parsed attacker object shaped as a VNode and carrying `constructor: null` passes the gate. If an application passes that unsanitized object into the render tree, Preact consumes its attacker-controlled type and props as a VNode and can inject HTML, with script execution possible where CSP or other defenses do not stop it. The companion loose `childVNode.constructor == UNDEFINED` check also admits null as the VNode sentinel in child processing. The server-side preact-render-to-string path was not affected.

causal_chain.bug_semantics: An attacker can place OSC/CSI control bytes in a filesystem entry name. When a user scans that entry in `dua i`, marks it, and quits without deleting it, the marked `PathBuf` is taken from the TUI mark pane. After `drop(terminal)` has restored the real terminal, the program passed `path.display()` directly to `println!`. No encoding or control-character filtering occurred at that output boundary, so a terminal emulator interpreted the embedded bytes rather than displaying an inert path, enabling such effects as terminal-title spoofing or clipboard manipulation.

That commit first created both the attacker-controlled path flow and the unsanitized post-TUI terminal sink; its immediate parent contains neither the extraction helper nor this print loop.

causal_chain.bug_semantics: An authenticated backend user with backend.manage_editor could save attacker-controlled LESS in Editor Settings -> Markup Styles. EditorSetting::compileCss() concatenated html_custom_styles into a .fr-view rule and returned Less_Parser output; LESS escaped-string syntax such as ~"</style><script>alert(1)</script><style>" preserved HTML delimiters. After the output-side strip_tags() call was removed, _custom_styles.php embedded that compiled string verbatim inside a <style> element used by the normal and authentication backend layouts, allowing stored CSS to terminate the style element and execute script when another backend user loaded a page.
causal_chain.flaw_origin: Commit c9dab67bc819b791df8432a898dd976f19388a87 changed only the exception path to e($ex->getMessage()) in EditorSetting::renderCss(), but simultaneously replaced <?= strip_tags(EditorSetting::renderCss()) ?> with the raw <?= EditorSetting::renderCss() ?> sink in modules/backend/layouts/_custom_styles.php. Escaping exception text did not sanitize successfully compiled, attacker-controlled LESS output, so this commit removed the defense from the successful compilation path without replacing it.

causal_chain.bug_semantics: A backend user holding backend.manage_branding can store attacker-controlled LESS in Settings -> Customize Backend -> Styles. BrandSetting::compileCss() concatenates custom_css into the LESS input; LESS escape syntax such as ~"</style><script>alert(1)</script><style>" preserves HTML delimiter and script text in the compiled result. BrandSetting::renderCss() returned that result without HTML sanitization, and modules/backend/layouts/_custom_styles.php echoed it inside a <style> element on backend pages, so the stored </style> breakout executes script for backend viewers.

The immediate parent already had the custom_css settings field and the style sink, but did not feed custom_css into the compiler, so this one-line data-flow addition is the smallest real BIC rather than later cache, rename, refactor, or error-handling commits.
