In 71a5dd67ab9e0d0da7caabd3fb5aaa3d86bb45e5 the CMS module simultaneously defined granular per-template permissions and exposed one controller guarded only by cms.*. Once any one CMS permission admitted a user, server-side handlers selected the object class solely from attacker-controlled type/templateType values; UI side-menu restrictions were therefore not authorization. The same constructor always bound AssetList, and its upload processor accepted files without the theme check used by its other mutations. Commit 55848e400cea002491a29820e5387bce0dd44362 is not the BIC: its parent is already vulnerable, and its change from cms.* to the explicit five permissions only excludes manage_themes-only users while retaining any-one-permission entry. Fix 164c62524e8abc153d09c6c35916278bdb746a2b closes the lifecycle at both layers by registering only authorized widgets, mapping each type to its required permission and enforcing it in every relevant handler, and validating the upload theme. causal_chain.bug_semantics: The CMS controller admitted a backend user possessing any one CMS Theme Editor permission, but its AJAX handlers trusted the request-controlled template type and did not re-check the permission mapped to that type. A pages-only user could therefore open, create, save, delete, commit, or reset partials, layouts, content, or assets by crafting the handler parameters. The constructor also registered every template widget, including AssetList, for every admitted CMS user; AssetList's upload path processed a file without first binding the request to the active theme, so a user without cms.manage_assets could reach an unauthorized upload into the active theme's assets.
causal_chain.flaw_origin: Single-parent commit 71a5dd67ab9e0d0da7caabd3fb5aaa3d86bb45e5 introduced the exploitable design as new code: modules/cms/controllers/Index.php used the section-wide cms.* gate, instantiated every TemplateList and AssetList unconditionally, and dispatched request-supplied type values into load/create/save/delete operations without a type-specific authorization check. The same commit introduced AssetList.php with constructor-time checkUploadPostback() upload processing and no validateRequestTheme() call in that upload path, while expanding modules/cms/ServiceProvider.php to register distinct cms.manage_content/assets/pages/layouts permissions. Its parent had only a skeletal CMS ServiceProvider and had neither Index.php nor AssetList.php, so the permission boundary and bypass surface first coexist in this commit.

reasoning: The advisory's attack requires both a self-service save path reachable by a user without backend.manage_users and a way for that path to accept fields reserved for an administrative user form. The latter pieces existed in the initial public code: the self-save handler targeted the current user, FormController let POST form_context override the trusted context, and Users conditionally added permission fields based on that context. They were latent for the stated low-privilege attacker while the Users controller required backend.manage_users. Commit 94a4ccb6abccd025e7e201590999061574ffdeb9 is therefore the smallest real BIC: it changes only the reachability guard and first makes mysettings available without permissions, completing the exploit path. Its direct parent retains the controller-wide backend.manage_users requirement and lacks the override, establishing parent absence. The BIC predates all affected 1.0/1.1/1.2 ranges, and the three branch-specific fix commits land exactly in the advisory's first patched tags. The fix removes client control of context and adds model-level authorization defense in depth. Because the BIC commit object is a 2014 human-authored/committed change with no AI or bot marker or trailer, the BIC-only attribution verdict is NOT_AI.

causal_chain.bug_semantics: An authenticated backend user could submit the self-service account save handler with an attacker-chosen form_context such as update. FormController trusted that POST value over the server-selected myaccount context, so Users::formExtendFields treated the request as an administrative user form and admitted role, individual-permission, and superuser-related fields into the form widget's save data. The handler still selected the attacker's own User model, allowing protected authorization attributes to be mass-updated and the account to gain higher backend privileges.

That small authorization change was the first point at which ordinary authenticated backend users could reach the already-existing unsafe composition of mysettings_onSave and POST-controlled FormController context selection; its parent still required backend.manage_users for the controller, so the low-privilege attack path was absent there.

causal_chain.bug_semantics: ScpClient.Download(string, DirectoryInfo) starts a recursive SCP receive and trusts the filename captured from each server-controlled C (file) or D (directory) protocol record. It joins that unvalidated value to the current local download directory and then creates the directory or opens the file for writing. A malicious, compromised, or MITM server can therefore supply ../ components (and, after the later Path.Combine form, rooted paths) to escape the caller's destination and create or overwrite any path writable by the client process. Exploitation requires the victim to initiate a recursive directory download from the attacker-controlled endpoint.
causal_chain.flaw_origin: Commit d96c93abb2f9409281bfb12d2da8622470a4b3e3 first added ScpClient and its recursive directory-download implementation. In Renci.SshClient/Renci.SshNet/ScpClient.NET.cs it parsed arbitrary remote C/D record names and used them directly in local directory creation and FileInfo construction without requiring a single safe path component. Commit 266dbaefe6c1f2bff2ea00c9ac14a246d37079d9 later changed the string concatenations to Path.Combine but did not introduce the trust-boundary flaw; renames, line-ending changes, and the 2023 partial-class merge likewise only carried the existing mechanism forward.

reasoning: The security defect is not that JDBC DataSource has a method named getConnection() by itself; it is the composition of c3p0's serializable, JavaBean-style DataSource objects, dangerous no-argument resource getters, and the absence of explicit BeanInfo suppressing those pseudo-properties. A deserialization carrier can therefore perform what appears to be a property read but actually opens a JDBC connection and executes driver code. Commit 7b022c4b6694dabc6204254dc917af9c38f2cb27 closes that route by generating and packaging explicit BeanInfo for all relevant implementations, excluding the methods by both property name and return type, and it is present starting in v0.14.0. For origin, git -S/grep/history inspection reaches 66e3716e788e0ac8f9c2e8e93711cfee301bede8, whose empty immediate parent lacks every vulnerable line. However, the commit message and tag prove that object is a reconstructed import of the complete 0.8.4-test1 source release, while the first-party 0.8 release archive documents the same serializable JavaBean DataSource design two years earlier. Treating the import or the separate 2012 Git migration root as the BIC would violate the protocol's ban on release/squash aggregates. Because the pre-0.8 development history needed to identify the smallest commit is absent, there is no genuine BIC commit object on which to make an AI-only judgment; this is a genuine public-history boundary and therefore BLOCKED rather than NOT_AI or EVIDENCE_GAP.

causal_chain.bug_semantics: A deserialization gadget carrier that performs JavaBeans property reads, most notably a collection sorted by Apache Commons BeanUtils BeanComparator, can treat the no-argument JDBC methods getConnection() and getPooledConnection() as readable properties named connection and pooledConnection. If an attacker-controlled serialized c3p0 DataSource or ConnectionPoolDataSource is configured to reach a susceptible JDBC driver, the property read invokes that driver-facing method during deserialization and can trigger the driver's dangerous behavior.
causal_chain.flaw_origin: c3p0 made its JDBC DataSource implementations Serializable and deliberately JavaBean-style while exposing public no-argument getConnection()/getPooledConnection() methods, but shipped no explicit BeanInfo that excluded those resource-producing methods from introspection. The vulnerable combination is already present in c3p0's first public 0.8 release, before the repository's reconstructed Git history begins, so the development commit that originated it is not publicly represented.

reasoning: The vulnerability is not merely that Typebot intentionally supports scripts; it is a missing trust transition. PR #194 made imported JSON executable in the authenticated preview origin by carrying block content through codeToExecute to a raw Function call. That gives an imported attacker's code the victim's builder origin and session, from which the credential-list/get endpoints provide the confidentiality impact described by the GHSA. Line history proves later AsyncFunction conversion, renames, and refactors preserved the same unsandboxed mechanism. PR #194 was squash-merged, so treating landed 1a3869ae6d9fa92fc71ef9d981bfffb8e4ee4ecc as irreducible would be wrong; the public PR exposes one original member, 3487850b9f4808617d347ddde4d9701f56662894, whose tree and parent exactly equal the landed squash tree and parent. That member is therefore the smallest reconstructable BIC. Its immediate parent has no packages/js executor path, while the BIC creates the importer, server dispatch, and Function sink together. The identical landed tree is present before the first @typebot.io/js release and remains in 0.9.14. Fix a68f0c91790af8f52f17557f4aa202e966e7e579 directly establishes an imported-code trust flag and a credentialless worker for preview, and it is the sole relevant boundary commit between js-v0.9.14 and js-v0.9.15. Finally, the BIC commit object contains only human Baptiste Arnaud authorship/committer identity and no AI marker, so under BIC-only attribution the closed verdict is NOT_AI.

causal_chain.bug_semantics: An attacker-controlled Typebot imported from JSON could retain a Script block whose content the preview API returned as a client-side action. @typebot.io/js then compiled that untrusted content with Function/AsyncFunction directly in the authenticated builder page. Code run there could make same-origin fetch requests with the victim's session, enumerate the victim's user/workspace credentials, receive decrypted credential data from credentials.getCredentials, and exfiltrate API keys, OAuth tokens, and passwords. The workspace form of getCredentials also authorized the supplied workspace but, at the vulnerable snapshot, did not bind the requested credential ID to that workspace.
causal_chain.flaw_origin: The single member commit behind PR #194 introduced all three causal pieces together: file import accepted JSON.parse(fileContent) without marking executable blocks untrusted, the viewer converted Script/Code block content into a codeToExecute client action, and the new @typebot.io/js executeCode implementation invoked Function on that content in the page context. It supplied neither a trust boundary for imported bots nor a sandbox/credentialless execution context.

The repository nevertheless proves a real, remotely relevant template-code-execution primitive in the affected lifecycle. Commit 2afc2aa5c29a413db5bf26fb0ef39fc6a18fec78 is the first commit that lets arbitrary dotted `{{ ... }}` expressions reach Python eval; a context-rooted payload traverses `__class__`, `__mro__`, and `__subclasses__` despite empty globals. Direct comparison with parent 04922ab0ea7f509c9c6cbcc1eca1fbab60d6fd1d proves that interpolation path absent there. The sink survives a module split in c539c2a5c3bfb0e07d41b35a0e4b1cf3fb51b89a and is reimplemented unsafely in 806f68cdab59694b780f3af0f0a6f7a535bbd08d for v0.2.0-alpha. That fix removes the raw evaluator and blocks private attribute traversal in an AST interpreter. The causal/AI judgment is closed; only distribution of the already-committed fix remains open.

causal_chain.bug_semantics: Attacker-controlled template expressions were evaluated as Python with a live rendering context. In the 0.1.x interpolation path, `{{ x.__class__.__mro__[1].__subclasses__() }}` passed a context-rooted dotted expression to raw `eval`; an empty globals dictionary is not a sandbox, because Python attribute traversal from any ordinary context object reaches the process object graph and can recover classes, module globals, and command-execution primitives. The 0.2.0-alpha rewrite retained the defect: `ExpressionEvaluator` either walked arbitrary attributes/methods or routed expressions containing an operator to `safe_eval`, which called raw `eval` with only `__builtins__` emptied. Commit 62c95c472fbd9ca5630a989ddec9d8899256726a replaced those paths with an AST interpreter that rejects underscore-prefixed attributes and restricts callable methods/builtins.
causal_chain.flaw_origin: The smallest real BIC for the reported `{{ ... }}` SSTI path is 2afc2aa5c29a413db5bf26fb0ef39fc6a18fec78 (`Add the possibility to call variables methods in the template`). It widened both interpolation regexes from simple `\w+` names to arbitrary expressions and added `variable_value = eval(".".join(expression), {}, context)` in `pyblade/engine/parser.py`. Its immediate parent only looked up a simple captured name and could not send dotted interpolation syntax to Python evaluation. The later c539c2a5c3bfb0e07d41b35a0e4b1cf3fb51b89a split/moved this same sink to `pyblade/engine/parsing/variables.py`, and 806f68cdab59694b780f3af0f0a6f7a535bbd08d replaced it with another unsafe evaluator for 0.2.0-alpha; neither later commit is the origin. The issue's separate assertion that `_is_safe_ast` in 0.1.8-alpha accepts a Constant-rooted `''.__class__` payload is contradicted by that tag's tree and by execution: the Attribute branch returns false unless the base is an allowed Name/attribute pair, and the sandbox is not called by the tagged rendering path. The real 0.1.x sink is the context-rooted interpolation eval above.

causal_chain.bug_semantics: An EventStream subscriber was authorized only at dashboard-subscription granularity, then placed in a global client registry. OnExecutionStarted, OnExecutionFinished, and OnOutputChunk iterated that registry and sent every execution event to every subscriber without applying acl.IsAllowedLogs for the recipient and action. The finished-event LogEntry included the command's accumulated Output, while OutputChunk exposed live bytes, so a low-privileged authenticated dashboard user could observe metadata and output for an action whose logs that user was not authorized to view.
causal_chain.flaw_origin: Commit a62d58f11955fe192f45da13e23ba996a2759404 introduced the ConnectRPC EventStream path itself in service/internal/api/api.go and proto/olivetin/api/v1/olivetin.proto. In that same commit, EventStream registered a user-bearing client globally; OnExecutionStarted, OnExecutionFinished, and OnOutputChunk broadcast to every registered client; and internalLogEntryToPb copied logEntry.Output into the response. The immediate parent had no ConnectRPC EventStream implementation. This was a new independently vulnerable transport path, not merely the later movement of already-vulnerable lines: a legacy WebSocket broadcaster existed separately and was later ACL-fixed by 4e7273b616245d60626b51a291edd97ab8ef53bc without touching service/internal/api/api.go, leaving the EventStream path vulnerable.

reasoning: The security boundary is server-side SID validity, not possession of the browser's current cookie jar. Before the BIC, local authentication already created a random SID, retained it for about one year, and authenticated any request presenting a SID found in SessionStorage, while Logout was only a nonfunctional stub. The BIC implemented the first apparent-success logout behavior: the UI called Logout and the API expired the browser cookie, but the commit never deleted the same SID from storage. Therefore a copied pre-logout cookie continued through GetUserSession and restored the user's identity. The exact vulnerable clear-cookie-only lines are absent from the immediate parent and first appear in the single-parent BIC; subsequent edits only expanded or hardened cookie clearing. The direct advisory fix finally passes the authenticated provider/SID to provider-specific revocation before cookie removal and is contained from release 3000.11.1 onward. Because the smallest BIC's own commit object is human-authored and contains no AI signal, the lifecycle is proven and the correct BIC-only verdict is NOT_AI.

Authentication continued to resolve a replayed SID through GetUserSession until its roughly one-year expiry, so anyone retaining the old cookie remained authenticated after the user appeared to log out; the same design later also cleared the OAuth2 cookie without deleting its server-side state.

causal_chain.bug_semantics: The unauthenticated GET /images handler accepts request.query.src and passes it to imageProcessor. For any value beginning with http:// or https://, imageProcessor treats it as external, skips all local-path validation, and calls fetch(src) without a destination allowlist or network-address restriction. An attacker can therefore make the EverShop server request attacker-selected external or internal HTTP(S) resources, including link-local metadata services, producing blind SSRF.

Its newly written external-URL branch classified a URL only by its http/https prefix and then directly executed fetch(src); the validation in the same function applied only to non-external filesystem paths. This is the first repository commit that contains both the public request path and the flawed server-side fetch mechanism, not a later move, refactor, revert, or release aggregate.

An attacker can therefore make the EverShop server request attacker-selected external or internal HTTP(S) resources, including link-local metadata services, producing blind SSRF.
audit_record.flaw_origin: Commit 5ed5ba31913ae69d617089988aa4ffe8015d6143 created both the front-store images handler and imageProcessor.ts. Its newly written external-URL branch classified a URL only by its http/https prefix and then directly executed fetch(src); the validation in the same function applied only to non-external filesystem paths. This is the first repository commit that contains both the public request path and the flawed server-side fetch mechanism, not a later move, refactor, revert, or release aggregate.

evidence: The assigned GHSA describes unauthenticated blind SSRF through GET /images?src=... in @evershop/evershop <=2.1.0 and records no first_patched_version. Its referenced researcher analysis identifies packages/evershop/src/modules/cms/services/imageProcessor.ts and the direct fetch(src) call; public issue https://github.com/evershopcommerce/evershop/issues/928 independently gives the concrete metadata request GET /images?src=http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/ and calls the endpoint public.

At tag v2.1.0, packages/evershop/src/modules/cms/pages/frontStore/images/images.ts reads request.query.src and passes it to imageProcessor. In packages/evershop/src/modules/cms/services/imageProcessor.ts, lines 74-75 recognize only the http/https prefix, lines 177-204 enter the external branch and call fetch(src), and lines 210-211 consume the response body. The local-path restrictions are confined to the !isExternalUrl branch.

git log -L 202,211:packages/evershop/src/modules/cms/services/imageProcessor.ts v2.1.0 follows the vulnerable fetch block directly to new-file commit 5ed5ba31913ae69d617089988aa4ffe8015d6143. git blame -L 74,77 -L 177,211 v2.1.0 attributes the classifier and entire external-fetch block to the same commit. git log --all -S'const response = await fetch(src)' for that path returns only its addition in 5ed5ba31913ae69d617089988aa4ffe8015d6143 and removal in fix af6e6fd935c4194668b11a924b847542598941f7.

git show 5ed5ba31913ae69d617089988aa4ffe8015d6143 shows both packages/evershop/src/modules/cms/pages/frontStore/images/images.ts and packages/evershop/src/modules/cms/services/imageProcessor.ts added from /dev/null. The commit is an ordinary single-parent commit whose direct parent is 753e8aeac5e7a9753731a8ad0f449c05cb2fa61e; no member/squash series is exposed to decompose.

Direct parent-tree verification: git cat-file -e 753e8aeac5e7a9753731a8ad0f449c05cb2fa61e:packages/evershop/src/modules/cms/services/imageProcessor.ts fails because the path is absent, and the identical check for packages/evershop/src/modules/cms/pages/frontStore/images/images.ts also fails. Thus neither the vulnerable fetch implementation nor its /images request handler exists in the immediate parent.

Version boundary: git merge-base --is-ancestor 5ed5ba31913ae69d617089988aa4ffe8015d6143 v2.0.1 exits 1, while git tag --contains 5ed5ba31913ae69d617089988aa4ffe8015d6143 lists v2.1.0, v2.1.1, v2.1.2, and v2.2.1. The BIC therefore lands after v2.0.1 and before the advisory's affected v2.1.0 release. The later v2.1.1 and v2.1.2 tags also retain the vulnerable history, consistent with the advisory having no patched version and not being updated for later releases.

The fix commit adds packages/evershop/src/lib/util/secureFetch.ts with a default-deny IMAGE_ALLOWED_HOSTS allowlist, http/https parsing, and a guarded undici connector for every connection/redirect, then replaces fetch(src) with secureFetch(src) in imageProcessor.ts. This directly removes arbitrary-destination fetching for untrusted src values.

Patched boundary in available Git history: af6e6fd935c4194668b11a924b847542598941f7 is not an ancestor of tag v2.1.2 (git merge-base --is-ancestor exits 1); git tag --contains af6e6fd935c4194668b11a924b847542598941f7 lists v2.2.1, whose annotated tag resolves to commit 89d09fbd200931daa892c59ee8e5866490788e4c. reasoning: The vulnerable mechanism is the unbounded SVG rasterization policy, not merely Sharp usage or the later route file. History was therefore traced from the advisory-named branch: 5ed5ba31913ae69d617089988aa4ffe8015d6143 is the smallest commit that first wrote the unsafe SVG configuration and the handler-to-processor flow; a839543becedb75324a16c38194eb4c64ba5f635 only makes the already-written flow reachable at GET /images. The exact BIC parent tree lacks both relevant source files, directly proving parent absence. The v2.0.1/v2.1.0 tree boundary proves the feature first enters the advisory's affected release line. causal_chain.bug_semantics: The unauthenticated GET /images endpoint accepts an image source and sends the resulting bytes to Sharp. For SVG input, imageProcessor deliberately rasterizes at density 300 with limitInputPixels disabled and performs no structural bound on use-element shadow-tree depth or pattern-tile dimensions. A crafted SVG can therefore make the underlying SVG renderer consume unbounded CPU or memory until the application server, and potentially the host, is denied service.
causal_chain.flaw_origin: Commit 5ed5ba31913ae69d617089988aa4ffe8015d6143 first added packages/evershop/src/modules/cms/services/imageProcessor.ts and its unsafe SVG branch, including density: 300 and limitInputPixels: false, plus the request handler that passes attacker-selected src into the processor. Its immediate child a839543becedb75324a16c38194eb4c64ba5f635 registered that handler as public GET /images; the first affected release v2.1.0 contains both commits. The root-cause lines themselves originate in 5ed5ba31913ae69d617089988aa4ffe8015d6143, so the later route-enablement commit is lifecycle context rather than the BIC.

reasoning: The vulnerability began as an authorization regression, not with the original GraphQL endpoint. Commit 44a884b59e51d29f5022aa5b482b6c12e56ebfaa initially loaded an order only when its numeric ID matched and either customer_id matched tokenPayload.customerId or sid matched tokenPayload.sid. The immediate parent of the selected BIC still has those constraints. Commit 685f3baf290024133c45986100fc7296ee14c85e deliberately converted the public argument to a string UUID and simultaneously removed both identity predicates, making possession of an order UUID sufficient. causal_chain.bug_semantics: picklescan disassembles pickle GLOBAL/STACK_GLOBAL references and, in the default scan result, counts a finding only when the referenced module/name matches its hard-coded unsafe-globals blocklist. Through v0.0.34 the blocklist omitted both the serialized global _io.FileIO and urllib.request.urlopen, so a crafted pickle could open an arbitrary local file and pass that file object as the body of an attacker-directed HTTP request without either global being counted as dangerous. A consumer relying on the scan could then deserialize the payload, causing arbitrary file read plus SSRF/data exfiltration.
causal_chain.flaw_origin: The initial scanner implementation introduced the incomplete-denylist security model: src/picklescan/scanner.py enumerated selected suspicious globals and scan_pickle_bytes incremented issues_count only for exact blocklist matches, silently leaving unlisted callable globals such as _io.FileIO and urllib.request.urlopen outside the failing result. Later classification of unknown globals as Suspicious did not cure the default-pass behavior because only Dangerous globals incremented issues_count; the vulnerable mechanism therefore originates in the initial scanner commit rather than in a later refactor or blocklist expansion.

The unsafe-path check examines the still-encoded resource_name, but the filesystem branch subsequently calls url2pathname(resource_name), so percent escapes such as %2e%2e become .. only after validation. os.path.join(path_, '../...') then resolves outside path_; os.path.exists() accepts the escaped target, find() returns a FileSystemPathPointer, and load()/open() reads the arbitrary process-readable file. causal_chain.bug_semantics: OpenAM 16.0.6 installs the iPlanetDirectoryPro SSO cookie with com.sun.identity.cookie.httponly=false and com.iplanet.am.cookie.secure=false and without a SameSite default. Its OAuth2/OIDC consent path also exposed that same session identifier to JavaScript and treated it as the csrf form value. Consequently, same-origin script execution could read and replay the bearer session, and could satisfy the consent check with the stolen session identifier; the missing SameSite and protocol-derived Secure defaults widened cross-site and transport exposure.

causal_chain.bug_semantics: The authenticated chat-user endpoint accepts q after only trimming it and requiring two characters, then Chat::searchUsers() applies the database driver's ordinary SQL-string escape and interpolates the result into LOWER(ud.display_name) LIKE '%%%s%%'. SQL-string escaping prevents a quote breakout but leaves the LIKE pattern metacharacters % and _ active. Thus q=%% or q=__ passes the length gate and broadens the predicate instead of searching for those literal characters, letting any logged-in user retrieve active users' IDs and display names and systematically enumerate accounts.
causal_chain.flaw_origin: Commit a7275859a5d6bc19c20827fe1ec6f6d925ea6f27 introduced the chat feature, the authenticated user-search controller, and Chat::searchUsers() together. Its first implementation put attacker-controlled search text, protected only by the generic database escape(), inside a LIKE pattern and supplied neither wildcard escaping nor an SQL ESCAPE clause. Commit 1dd0432a900d85f712b26c6be07dd5f70511d868 later made the comparison case-insensitive and removed the is_visible restriction, but retained the already-flawed escape-plus-LIKE design; it expanded/rewrote the vulnerable search rather than originating the wildcard-injection mechanism.

causal_chain.bug_semantics: An administrator-controlled RSE creation request can persist HTML/JavaScript in the city, country_name, or ISP metadata fields. The WebUI then treats those stored strings as markup in two victim-facing paths: lib/rucio/web/ui/static/rses.js passes the raw API objects directly to DataTables columns, and lib/rucio/web/ui/static/rse.js concatenates metadata values into HTML passed to jQuery.append. Loading the RSE Management list or an RSE detail page therefore executes the stored payload in the viewer's WebUI origin, where it can read JavaScript-accessible session/token material and act with the victim's authority.
causal_chain.flaw_origin: Commit 8f1a24a568331b10f9d8fb099ef233af340b7735 introduced the RSE-management WebUI feature as one ordinary commit. It added the create form and POST client for raw city/country_name/ISP values, the /rse, /rses, and /rses/add UI routes, the listing DataTable whose data source is the unencoded server response, and the detail-table helper that interpolates returned values into HTML. The persistence API predated or existed independently of the browser view, but this commit first created the executable rendering sinks and the documented WebUI create/trigger lifecycle.

causal_chain.bug_semantics: An attacker who can add an account identity can POST an identity string containing HTML or JavaScript to /accounts/<account>/identities. The backend stores that identity string and the account-identities GET endpoint returns it. On the WebUI account page, load_identities handed the returned objects directly to jQuery DataTables as data and selected the identity and type properties as columns. DataTables treated those string values as cell HTML, so merely viewing the affected account page inserted the persisted identity into the DOM and executed attacker-controlled script in the viewer's WebUI origin.
causal_chain.flaw_origin: Commit 4f67434304e5bd445c01a636d88113b76a68ef78 created the account-administration page and lib/rucio/web/ui/static/account.js. Its new load_identities function passed the server response directly to DataTable with `data: data` and `columns: [{'data': 'identity'}, {'data': 'type'}]`, without encoding the identity before the HTML sink. The same feature commit also added the UI's identity-creation helper, completing the store-and-render path. The pre-existing backend identity model/API stored and returned the supplied identity as data; the vulnerability began when this commit added the unsafe browser rendering, not when later code was moved or refactored.

Vulnerable flow at the fix parent: lib/rucio/web/rest/flaskapi/v1/accounts.py parses the POST identity and calls add_account_identity, while its GET generator serializes every result of list_identities; lib/rucio/core/identity.py add_identity assigns the supplied string directly to models.Identity.identity. reasoning: The security boundary is the construction of a backend query string, not merely the later helper method. The smallest affected-history commit that first made attacker-controlled metadata keys reach such a sink is 9334d7d..., which simultaneously introduced the Elasticsearch converter's unescaped doKey() and the queryString sink. The earlier similar Azure converter is not the BIC for this advisory because it enforces an allowedIdentifierNames whitelist and is not one of the affected products; 9334d7d... removed that safety in the newly affected backend. OpenSearch and GemFire are later ports of the same causal design. Refactors in 2026 centralized escaping and a partial hardening added ordinary-space handling, but the vulnerable capability already existed and the last vulnerable tags still failed to escape alternate whitespace. Both supported release lines then received the same four-character escaping patch at the documented fixed boundaries. The immediate parent lacks the affected converter and sink, the BIC predates both affected version lines, and the BIC commit object has no AI attribution signal; therefore the BIC-only verdict is NOT_AI.

causal_chain.bug_semantics: The Elasticsearch, OpenSearch, and GemFire vector-store converters serialize a caller-supplied Filter.Key into a Lucene-style query string. Their escaping left tab, LF, CR, and U+3000 ideographic space unescaped, so a key can introduce token boundaries and operators such as OR; the resulting string is passed to the backend query parser, allowing an attacker to replace the intended metadata predicate with arbitrary query clauses.
causal_chain.flaw_origin: Commit 9334d7d540f8d0ee7cb09e44b272c95c2c159627 first added an affected backend and the causal pattern: ElasticsearchAiSearchFilterExpressionConverter.doKey() appended the metadata-prefixed Filter.Key directly to the query string with only trim(), while ElasticsearchVectorStore supplied that converted string to Elasticsearch queryString(). OpenSearch later copied the affected converter in 46e47849cec4b8a6fffbd13997f3cce4f886347b, and GemFire added the same kind of filter-query path in 833a856f51090f0eb98332db2341ce7a107af1fd. Later shared-converter refactors and partial escaping changed the location and reduced the character set but did not create the vulnerability or close the whitespace bypass.

In the validated full-history clone, git log -L 86,95:vector-stores/spring-ai-elasticsearch-store/src/main/java/org/springframework/ai/vectorstore/ElasticsearchAiSearchFilterExpressionConverter.java 9334d7d... resolves the raw doKey implementation to the new-file commit 9334d7d540f8d0ee7cb09e44b272c95c2c159627; git log -S 'context.append(prefixedIdentifier.trim()).append(":");' confirms 9334d7d... added that statement and later fc1f92d11cacc79bdf8d41eb7f941a64fdf67482 only moved/refactored it. The BIC also added vector-stores/spring-ai-elasticsearch-store/src/main/java/org/springframework/ai/vectorstore/ElasticsearchVectorStore.java, whose getElasticsearchSimilarityQuery() sends getElasticsearchQueryString(filterExpression) into queryString(...). Direct parent-tree check `git cat-file -e 8e50802eb8dd9044c15d7e75ad94ae618dca5c12:vector-stores/spring-ai-elasticsearch-store/src/main/java/org/springframework/ai/vectorstore/ElasticsearchAiSearchFilterExpressionConverter.java` fails because the path is absent, while the BIC adds it from /dev/null. audit_record.reasoning: The security boundary is the construction of a backend query string, not merely the later helper method. The smallest affected-history commit that first made attacker-controlled metadata keys reach such a sink is 9334d7d..., which simultaneously introduced the Elasticsearch converter's unescaped doKey() and the queryString sink. The earlier similar Azure converter is not the BIC for this advisory because it enforces an allowedIdentifierNames whitelist and is not one of the affected products; 9334d7d... removed that safety in the newly affected backend. OpenSearch and GemFire are later ports of the same causal design. Refactors in 2026 centralized escaping and a partial hardening added ordinary-space handling, but the vulnerable capability already existed and the last vulnerable tags still failed to escape alternate whitespace. Both supported release lines then received the same four-character escaping patch at the documented fixed boundaries. The immediate parent lacks the affected converter and sink, the BIC predates both affected version lines, and the BIC commit object has no AI attribution signal; therefore the BIC-only verdict is NOT_AI.

reasoning: The lifecycle has two distinct stages. The volume-target PATCH response was introduced in Ironic's 9.0-era endpoint work and continued returning the complete updated object, but its authorization was system-scoped, so that response shape alone did not let a caller with update permission cross a separate target-secret visibility boundary. The smallest commit that made the advisory's exploit real is e870bd34: it opened update operations to project-scoped owner/lessee roles and, in the same commit, defined a narrower policy for viewing target properties. It correctly enforced that new policy on GET/list yet omitted it from PATCH, leaving a lower-privileged updater able to recover pre-existing properties by changing another field. The immediate parent has neither the view-properties policy nor project-scoped volume update, directly proving absence. The BIC is in 17.0.0 but not 16.0.5, which exactly matches the advisory's security boundary. dd2df520 and its backports close both layers by enforcing PATCH redaction and masking password-like property values during serialization; the 29.0.6/29.0.5 ancestry checks confirm a concrete patched boundary. Finally, the raw e870bd34 commit object is human-authored/committed and has no AI marker. Claude attribution exists only on the later fix and cannot attribute the BIC, so the closed verdict is NOT_AI.

causal_chain.bug_semantics: A project-scoped caller who is authorized to PATCH a volume target but is not authorized by baremetal:volume:view_target_properties can modify an unrelated allowed field and receive the complete updated VolumeTarget in the HTTP 200 response. The PATCH path serializes new_target with convert_with_links() without applying the view-target-properties redaction used by GET/list, so properties that can hold iSCSI connection details and credentials are disclosed. POST has the same unredacted serialization shape, but the requester supplied those values; the security-relevant information gain identified by the bundle is PATCH, where an otherwise-authorized edit reveals pre-existing secrets.
causal_chain.flaw_origin: Commit e870bd34d0ccacbaef7f4e4def2535eb28f822b9 created the exploitable authorization split. It expanded baremetal:volume:update to system and project scopes (including owner members/lessee admins), introduced the stricter baremetal:volume:view_target_properties policy, and added that policy's redaction to GET/list only. It left PATCH returning convert_with_links(new_target) without the new redaction check. The unredacted PATCH response itself originated with the volume-target API in c380e05dbf84079b01fb3b0ea099ef9b293b9b3d and was mechanically rewritten by 000bc72cc29b8637df496f2e6768281606a27058, but neither is the security BIC: before e870bd34 the update endpoint was system-scoped and there was no distinct lower privilege that could update while being denied target properties.

Therefore the parent retained an unredacted response but did not permit the project-scoped update-without-view privilege combination; the vulnerable authorization differential is absent in the immediate parent.

causal_chain.bug_semantics: The MCP-exposed ado installer accepted an attacker-controlled package name and interpolated it into executable Stata source without validation or quoting. A package containing a newline therefore terminated the intended `ssc install` command and introduced another Stata command; Stata's `shell`/`!` escape then executed an arbitrary OS command with the server process's privileges. In the advisory-era implementation, `ado_package_install` forwarded `package` through `SSC_Install.install()` to `StataController.run()`/`pexpect.sendline()`; in the original implementation, the same untrusted value was written into a `.do` file and that file was executed by Stata.
causal_chain.flaw_origin: b61cd574b86bb6aa3a931ed637de0fb66ce82607 first added the MCP tool `ssc_install(command, is_replace)` in `src/stata_mcp/__init__.py`: lines 646-650 interpolated `command` directly into `write_dofile(f"ssc install {command}...")` and immediately passed the resulting file to `stata_do`. The immediate parent had no SSC-install tool or SSC command construction. Later commits moved the server code and replaced this implementation with the `ado_package_install(package)`/`SSC_Install.install(package)` framework, preserving the same missing trust-boundary validation rather than originating it.

reasoning: The vulnerability begins with the old-format PyTorch feature itself. PyTorch establishes format validity by unpickling its first object, but the new picklescan implementation substituted a syntactic search for a literal integer opcode and rejected the file before scanning payload pickles when that search failed. The immediate parent lacks both the helper file and the old-format scan function, while the BIC adds the complete flawed mechanism in one ordinary, single-parent commit, making f98f9bd89b16ab1b1b1b6366acddd1b2a4d36fe9 smaller and more causal than subsequent error-handling or routing commits. The dynamic-REDUCE reproduction demonstrates that a valid PyTorch magic value can have no INT/LONG opcode, and the advisory demonstrates how a dangerous later pickle is consequently skipped. Tag containment puts the flaw in releases beginning with v0.0.3 and still in v1.0.2. The direct fix is the v1.0.3 tag commit: it treats a nonliteral magic as suspicious, scans and merges the first pickle's globals, and continues through the payload sequence. Finally, the BIC's raw commit object contains only a named human author/committer and no AI marker, so under the required BIC-only attribution rule the closed verdict is NOT_AI.

causal_chain.bug_semantics: Legacy PyTorch serialization unpickles the first pickle to obtain MAGIC_NUMBER, so that value may be computed by a REDUCE callable rather than encoded as an INT/LONG opcode. picklescan's get_magic_number instead disassembled the first pickle and returned only the first opcode whose name contained INT or LONG. An attacker could encode eval('0x1950A86A20F9469CFC6C') as the first pickle: PyTorch obtains the correct magic number, while picklescan obtains None and rejects/abandons the PyTorch scan before examining the later pickle containing the dangerous payload. The file therefore remains loadable by PyTorch while the scanner misses the code-execution globals.

causal_chain.bug_semantics: A pickle GLOBAL/STACK_GLOBAL for the module-level callable profile.run is parsed as module="profile", name="run". PickleScan classified a global as an issue only when the module appeared in its manually enumerated unsafe map and the extracted name exactly matched that module's filter (or the filter was "*"). The original map omitted profile entirely; a later attempted hardening used {"Profile.run", "Profile.runctx"}, which still could not match the extracted module-level names "run" and "runctx". Thus a malicious pickle could produce zero issues and then profile.run(statement) would reach Profile.run and exec(statement) when unpickled.
causal_chain.flaw_origin: The flaw originated in the first PickleScan implementation: it introduced an exact-name, manually enumerated dangerous-global filter without any entry for Python's profile module. causal_chain.bug_semantics: The optimized standard integer for-loop exposed its stack-local C++ counter to ChaiScript with var(&i). ChaiScript's intentional := reference-assignment could therefore copy an alias to that counter into a returned Boxed_Value. Once the compiled loop lambda returned, the counter's stack lifetime ended, but an escaping value (including one transported through async/future) retained the raw pointer; interpolation then reached Boxed_Number::get_as and dereferenced dangling storage, producing garbage, an invalid read, or a segmentation fault.
causal_chain.flaw_origin: Commit 683164650a462b6d5ea58bb899f4c2e668243a1d introduced the compiled-for-loop fast path and, within that new path, created int i on the lambda stack and registered var(&i). The existing reference-assignment semantics made the new stack-backed binding escapable. Later optimizer extraction and formatting commits only moved or reformatted this mechanism. The fix instead places the counter in an owning Boxed_Value and obtains the native int reference from that owned storage, so escaping aliases retain the allocation.

causal_chain.bug_semantics: A remote unauthenticated client can repeatedly submit candidate administrator passwords to either the Administration Console's /j_security_check flow or the Management REST /management/domain flow. Each request independently reaches credential verification, and a bad credential only produces the normal login failure/HTTP 401 response: the vulnerable implementation keeps no failure count across requests and applies no delay, throttle, concurrent-attempt cap, or account/host lockout. Consequently an attacker can make an unbounded series of guesses and a later correct password is still accepted.
causal_chain.flaw_origin: The smallest reconstructed code-origin commit is javaee/glassfish commit 0fee8143d3ad099bb7b4583785693957c838523a: it created RestAdapter.java as the remotely exposed, security-wrapped REST management adapter, called authenticate for every request, and returned an immediate 401 on failure without retaining or consulting any failed-attempt state. The later c1f1b2942b2a657eb61e707069dd4ea9d3e3a730 added AdminConsoleAuthModule.java and extended the same unrestricted behavior to the console login route. Eclipse commit 571714739b23e16c4c90d5229b806433920b3bcb is only the 2018 aggregate import of that already-vulnerable predecessor history, not the real BIC.

BIC reconstruction: `git show 0fee8143d3ad099bb7b4583785693957c838523a -- v3/admin/rest/src/main/java/org/glassfish/admin/rest/RestAdapter.java` in the archived public javaee/glassfish history shows a new 302-line adapter; service() calls authenticate before dispatch (original lines 113-148), authenticate(Request, ServerEnvironmentImpl) delegates each request to AdminAuthenticator (174-184), and a false result is immediately returned as HTTP 401 with WWW-Authenticate BASIC (212-230), with no attempt counter or backoff. `git cat-file -p 0fee8143d3ad099bb7b4583785693957c838523a` gives the sole parent 7975999a9bce3825ec4b162a92c1c51f00b0f4f1 and the stated human author/committer; `git ls-tree -r --name-only 7975999a9bce3825ec4b162a92c1c51f00b0f4f1 -- v3/admin/rest/src/main/java/org/glassfish/admin/rest/RestAdapter.java` returns no entry, directly proving parent-tree absence. `git show --stat c1f1b2942b2a657eb61e707069dd4ea9d3e3a730` shows the later one-file, 245-line addition of AdminConsoleAuthModule.java, and its parent 2dc31199f4f4963ed93fef32681248aa7c697901 likewise has no such path. `git tag --contains 0fee8143d3ad099bb7b4583785693957c838523a` includes 3.0.1, 3.1.2, 4.1.x, and 5.0.x; the vulnerable implementation was then imported into the Eclipse repository by root aggregate 571714739b23e16c4c90d5229b806433920b3bcb, well before affected 7.0.x. Immediately before the fix, `git blame -L 230,268 0a99606e18291a106b680b671cdfb97b2abab7be -- nucleus/admin/util/src/main/java/com/sun/enterprise/admin/util/GenericAdminAuthenticator.java` shows authService.login followed by success return or rethrow of LoginException, still without cross-request tracking. Merge commit https://github.com/eclipse-ee4j/glassfish/commit/6cab4ce3aad9bc65b52bc761a4aa88634a2bd0aa lands the completed fix series as PR https://github.com/eclipse-ee4j/glassfish/pull/26026, whose first-party description explicitly covers both the console and REST API. reasoning: Vulnerability-first tracing distinguishes the pre-existing network listener from the dangerous operation. Parent 805600159f34ca96d95c26c10c7b2799cb5951ce was reachable on all interfaces but its flow procedures deliberately threw NOT_IMPLEMENTED; aggregate 91ed3de52e7db92943886526395ad8eac6faa77f is the first persisted tree where an unauthenticated request can invoke the reflection server's action runner and obtain the result. Subsequent packaging moves and the 2025 explicit Express POST preserve that mechanism, while the 2026 localhost-CORS change cannot authorize requests and therefore does not remove DNS rebinding. The version graph places the origin before the first 0.5 release and the partial loopback mitigation only in 1.40.0, not at the CVE's claimed 2026-06-18 boundary. A complete Host-header/CORS patch is visible only on the still-open remediation PR. Most importantly for attribution, 91ed3de52e7db92943886526395ad8eac6faa77f is a squash aggregate and the audit protocol forbids treating it as the BIC. Its message makes the smaller causal member identifiable by subject, but neither its SHA nor its commit object is public/recoverable, so immediate-parent verification and commit-object AI inspection cannot be performed on the true BIC. That is a genuine public-history boundary, requiring BLOCKED rather than an AI or NOT_AI verdict.

causal_chain.bug_semantics: The unauthenticated Genkit developer Tools server accepted action-execution requests while listening beyond a loopback-only trust boundary and did not validate the HTTP Host header. CORS only controls which origins receive browser-readable response headers; it does not stop the handler, and a DNS-rebound page retains its attacker origin while resolving its hostname to the developer machine. Consequently a LAN client or DNS-rebound browser could reach the action runner, supply an action key and input (later also context), execute any registered flow/tool/model/prompt, and read the returned result. The reported chain also used the telemetry SSE endpoint's wildcard Access-Control-Allow-Origin to read trace inputs and outputs.
causal_chain.flaw_origin: The earliest persisted tree that makes the network-listening Runner API actually execute actions is squash aggregate 91ed3de52e7db92943886526395ad8eac6faa77f: it adds genkit-tools/src/runner/router.ts with a runAction mutation that proxies to the reflection server and changes genkit-tools/src/runner/runner.ts to expose that router through api.listen(port) without a host argument or Host validation. Its parent 805600159f34ca96d95c26c10c7b2799cb5951ce already had the all-interface Express listener but only stubbed, NOT_IMPLEMENTED flow operations, so it lacked the action-execution primitive. The squash message lists many member commits, including the causally relevant 'Implemented passthrough endpoints in Runner API', but that member commit object and SHA are not retained in the validated clone or associated public PR history; therefore the protocol's smallest non-aggregate BIC cannot be named.

causal_chain.bug_semantics: RustCrypto ml-dsa signature decoding used one monotonic() predicate for two different encodings. Hint cut offsets may repeat because an ML-DSA polynomial may contain no hints, but hint indices within each polynomial must be strictly increasing. Changing the shared predicate from < to <= made cuts valid but also accepted equal adjacent indices. A verifier therefore decoded a non-canonical signature containing a repeated hint index and could accept a byte-distinct malleation of a valid signature.

Wycheproof later supplied invalid repeated-hint vectors that exposed the regression.

causal_chain.bug_semantics: An authenticated board editor could send a single-block or batch PATCH naming a comment block created by another member. The handlers checked only the caller's general ability to manage board cards and the target block's board, then applied the caller-controlled patch; they never enforced comment ownership or the elevated permission for acting on other users' comments. This let an editor alter another member's comment and caused unauthorized integrity loss.

reasoning: The vulnerability is the authorization bypass in the existing-address routing-type augmentation, not generic STOMP auto-creation. Before the BIC, STOMP could auto-create a missing address through ServerSession (and its security boundary), but it did not mutate an existing address to satisfy a mismatched routing type; checkRoutingSemantics rejected that request. ARTEMIS-1794 commit d773e8f66b5db2b0fcaa646384c24690d38aaa69 deliberately enabled two STOMP routing types on the same address and introduced the smallest causal branch: it directly changed the broker's AddressInfo outside ServerSession authorization. The exact sink is absent from its immediate parent and is present beginning with release 2.6.0. Later refactors retain the same mechanism, so they are not introducers. ARTEMIS-5996 commit 53173375c4d5e4b57890e89d37ed8b666c974474 is the direct fix: it deletes the duplicated STOMP mutation logic and sends both attack paths through ServerSession.checkAutoCreate, whose createAddress path enforces CREATE_ADDRESS; its regression tests cover both send-only and consume-only credentials, and it lands in the first patched tag 2.54.0 after the sink remains in 2.53.0. Although the advisory conservatively lists versions back to 2.0.0, tag-level code establishes that this exact flaw begins in 2.6.0. Finally, the BIC commit object has no AI authorship or generation marker, so the causal result is NOT_AI.

causal_chain.bug_semantics: A STOMP client authenticated with only SEND or CONSUME permission could request a routing type that an existing address did not support. STOMP's auto-create path added that routing type by calling the broker server's updateAddressInfo directly, without the ServerSession CREATE_ADDRESS authorization check; the subsequent routing-semantics check then observed the newly added type and accepted the send or subscription. This let a low-privilege user mutate address routing configuration despite lacking createAddress permission.
causal_chain.flaw_origin: Commit d773e8f66b5db2b0fcaa646384c24690d38aaa69 added the first existing-address/missing-routing-type branch to StompConnection.autoCreateDestinationIfPossible. It copied the address's routing types, added the client-requested effectiveAddressRoutingType, and invoked manager.getServer().updateAddressInfo(...) directly. The parent only auto-created through the authenticated ServerSession when an address did not exist and otherwise left an unsupported routing type for checkRoutingSemantics to reject. Later edits moved or modernized the same sink but did not originate the authorization bypass.

causal_chain.bug_semantics: With address auto-creation disabled, an authenticated OpenWire client could request a non-durable JMS topic subscription on a nonexistent address while holding the queue-creation and consume permissions sufficient for the subscription but lacking CREATE_ADDRESS/createAddress permission. The 2.53.0 regression test grants CREATE_NON_DURABLE_QUEUE (the advisory prose calls the relevant permission createDurableQueue). The OpenWire topic path created a temporary subscription queue directly; that temporary queue creation also materialized the missing temporary address without the topic path first enforcing the address-existence/CREATE_ADDRESS check. The unauthorized address lived until the OpenWire connection closed.
causal_chain.flaw_origin: The original OpenWire consumer implementation sent topic subscriptions straight from AMQSession.createConsumer into AMQConsumer.init, where the non-durable branch generated a UUID queue name and called coreSession.createQueue(address, subQueueName, selector, true, false). Unlike the queue-destination branch added later, the topic branch never called the broker's auto-create preflight. In the affected implementation this mattered because ServerSessionImpl.createQueue conditioned its CREATE_ADDRESS security check on autoCreateAddresses, while ActiveMQServerImpl.createQueue separately materialized a missing address whenever the QueueConfiguration was temporary. Thus direct temporary queue creation could create its missing address with autoCreateAddresses=false, and the user's non-durable-queue permission reached implicit address creation without the required address permission.

causal_chain.bug_semantics: Bastillion's authentication filter was mapped only to /manage/* and /admin/*, while the lmvc controller dispatcher accepted any raw request URI containing an annotated controller path plus .ktrl. A request such as /anything/manage/viewUsers.ktrl therefore missed the prefix-scoped AuthFilter but was still substring-dispatched to the privileged /manage/viewUsers controller; unauthenticated attackers could read administrative data, create a MANAGER account, and register systems.
causal_chain.flaw_origin: The flawed routing primitive was first written in the lmvc framework's 2018 initial source commit: BaseKontroller.execute() used request.getRequestURI().contains(c.path() + DispatcherServlet.CTR_EXT). Bastillion first integrated that framework in 65475902748be6b86a95d17b8409518697fe1e77 while retaining prefix-only AuthFilter mappings, making the mismatch exploitable in the application. Later package renames, artifact releases, and the 2026 source import merely carried the same line forward.

reasoning: The unvalidated fetch sink and the signing behavior arrived as separate granular commits. dcbaefb0976cf3e9d9490455bb59504d5c807847 created proxy.php, but the endpoint rejected requests without a secret-derived hash, so that precursor alone did not give a BBCode author the advisory's SSRF primitive. The direct parent of a892a53ba45330d69b8ad8b1ede82aebaa29537b still has exactly that secret-gated state. The BIC then made untrusted [img] URLs flow through a server-side signing oracle, producing a browser-loadable local proxy request that reaches the unvalidated server fetch. Later refactoring and stronger HMAC authentication retained that causal data flow, and the April 2026 textual-host checks remained bypassable because they did not validate resolved addresses or redirects. The June/July 2026 branch fixes close the mechanism at the fetch layer and on redirects, with corresponding advisory merges for 3.0 and 2.1. The BIC is a normal, non-merge, non-squash human commit, its direct parent lacks the signing flow, and its commit object has no AI authorship marker. Any AI marker on a 2026 fix commit is out of scope for BIC attribution. Therefore the closed verdict is NOT_AI.

causal_chain.bug_semantics: When the image proxy is enabled, an authenticated poster can place an attacker-chosen non-HTTPS URL in a BBCode [img] tag. SMF's BBCode renderer converts that URL into a local proxy.php URL and generates the required secret-derived hash itself. A subsequent request to that local URL makes the forum server fetch the remote URL. Before the fixes, the fetch path did not resolve and reject private, loopback, link-local, or other reserved destination addresses on the initial request and every redirect, so an attacker-controlled hostname or redirect could make SMF request internal services, including link-local metadata endpoints.
causal_chain.flaw_origin: The proxy fetch endpoint was already present in the immediate parent and required a secret-derived hash, but was not yet an attacker-usable signing oracle. Commit a892a53ba45330d69b8ad8b1ede82aebaa29537b completed the vulnerable mechanism by adding BBCode-renderer code that accepts the untrusted image URL and automatically emits /proxy.php?request=<url>&hash=md5(<url>.<secret>) without any destination-address validation. This is the smallest commit that made the pre-existing unvalidated server-side fetch reachable with a valid signature from attacker-controlled BBCode.

git show a892a53ba45330d69b8ad8b1ede82aebaa29537b shows a one-file, nine-line change in Sources/Subs.php. In both BBCode img validators it adds image_proxy_enabled/image_proxy_secret/boardurl and rewrites each non-HTTPS image to $boardurl . '/proxy.php?request=' . urlencode($data) . '&hash=' . md5($data . $image_proxy_secret).

git log -L 1283,1308:Sources/Subs.php a892a53ba45330d69b8ad8b1ede82aebaa29537b identifies a892a53ba45330d69b8ad8b1ede82aebaa29537b as the commit that added those automatic proxy-signing lines; git log -S'/proxy.php?request=' over Sources/Subs.php likewise returns a892a53ba45330d69b8ad8b1ede82aebaa29537b as the initial signing change. The later 72b01034c2773bff3a6b9be6b859acce1b79f19f commit merely moved the same behavior into get_proxied_url().

Immediate-parent verification: git show 5c923a26d6c55060efdaf4d489403b06de8f65a1:Sources/Subs.php at the two img validators shows only URL normalization and no proxy.php rewrite, no secret use, and no hash generation. git show/cat-file also confirms that the parent already contains proxy.php, whose checkRequest() verifies md5($request . $this->secret) and whose cacheImage() performs the server-side curl fetch. Thus the signing-oracle attack path is absent in the direct parent even though its inert, secret-gated sink exists.

Lifecycle cross-check: 72b01034c2773bff3a6b9be6b859acce1b79f19f extracted the rewrite into get_proxied_url(); 8cecdb815e845f83a63e688250296ce90f35fcce changed the proxy hash from MD5 to HMAC but preserved automatic signing; c33589c13f9cfff339d2fe6874dcf6b8f15f643b later rejected literal IP hosts and localhost but still did not resolve hostnames or validate redirect destinations, so attacker-controlled DNS/redirects retained the SSRF.

At the vulnerable 2.1 pre-fix tree 3c98cab9b6ca9c247da4b43d2879dcb61c0af568, Sources/Subs.php's [img] validator calls get_proxied_url(); get_proxied_url() creates a valid HMAC-signed proxy URL; proxy.php verifies that HMAC and cacheImage() calls fetch_web_data($request). The only destination checks compare the textual host against a literal IP, localhost, and the forum host, leaving DNS-resolved private/link-local targets and redirects unchecked.

The 3.0 advisory merge 4bf35cf9e45573a5f55a6f52995086c1da89c096 has first parent 57d30d5a0ec32073d0dd1fe5b038d41dd84171b3 and second-parent tip ce59add4bdcacea557fb9a9763ad4b24d75a8a48. The seven-commit fix branch starts at 6d8b5f2d5ddf14b26bf6e9e0812db9327770902d and ends at ce59add4bdcacea557fb9a9763ad4b24d75a8a48; its final tree is identical to the merge tree. It centralizes resolved-IP safety checks in WebFetchApi and revalidates redirect targets in the curl/socket fetchers.

The parallel 2.1 advisory merge b4d23dfd74a511587c605f9d294cefc3a75b4b26 has first parent 3c98cab9b6ca9c247da4b43d2879dcb61c0af568 and direct second parent 10a998ccbae25bd95d4c3857a66a30b018bb5fda; its merge tree equals the direct parent's tree. That patch adds is_fetch_safe(), calls it before fetch_web_data() connects, rechecks curl redirects, and invokes it from proxy.php.

Version-boundary checks with git merge-base --is-ancestor succeed for BIC a892a53ba45330d69b8ad8b1ede82aebaa29537b -> v2.1.0 and -> v3.0-alpha.1. The BIC is also contained in every listed stable tag through v2.1.7 and in v3.0-alpha.1 through v3.0-alpha.4. The checks v2.1.7 -> b4d23dfd74a511587c605f9d294cefc3a75b4b26 and v3.0-alpha.4 -> 4bf35cf9e45573a5f55a6f52995086c1da89c096 also succeed, placing each fix after the last vulnerable release tag present in the clone.

reasoning: The vulnerability is the assignment operator in the authorization predicate, not the later file moves, class extraction, array-syntax modernization, namespace qualification, or the release merges. The line is demonstrably vulnerable in the last available affected tags and is corrected by the one-line direct commits on both maintained branches. Following the line backward through those semantic-preserving transformations reaches the sole Git root, where it already exists. That root imports 1,045 files and has no parent; treating it as a BIC would violate the protocol's requirement for the smallest commit that first wrote the flaw and would make immediate-parent absence impossible to verify. Since the retired external SVN history is the missing causal predecessor, this is a genuine public-history boundary rather than merely weak reachable evidence. No BIC commit object is available, so an AI/non-AI attribution cannot be made; fix-only and later commit metadata are irrelevant under the BIC-only rule.

causal_chain.bug_semantics: ApproveAttach obtains the boards on which the authenticated user has approve_posts permission, but its per-attachment predicate uses assignment instead of comparison: $allowed_boards = array(0) || in_array(...) (later [0] and \in_array). Because || binds more tightly than =, the non-empty array(0)/[0] left operand is truthy, short-circuits the membership test, and assigns boolean true to $allowed_boards; every queried pending attachment therefore passes the authorization gate. A low-privileged authenticated caller can consequently approve, reject, or delete pending attachments outside boards they may moderate.
causal_chain.flaw_origin: The vulnerable predicate predates the repository's accessible Git history. The sole Git root, a18e888838460a816fdbc2703e7e05ce7f626c91 (2012-01-24, message '10610'), is a 1,045-file whole-project snapshot and already contains the flawed line at Sources/ManageAttachments.php:1500. Later commits only preserve or move the same mechanism: 51ad4a4b2c1f7e292501f583d6defed62d56b535 renames ManageAttachments.php, 958840edad356bf237fd19790c36797d163cd383 extracts ApproveAttach into Sources/Actions/AttachmentApprove.php, a86ccb86190d867bd144a76a4c8d777e6c74a7b2 modernizes array(0) to [0], and 74e835324fbdbc594b2e67b068e548e541a163da qualifies in_array. None is the causal introducer. The pre-root SVN revision that first wrote the mistaken '=' cannot be reconstructed from the validated clone, and the legacy svn.simplemachines.org host no longer resolves.

Historical decomposition matters because main contains a GitHub squash commit: the exact PR head tree equals the squash landing tree, while the first recoverable member commit already adds every causal line and its immediate parent contains none of those files. That member is therefore the smallest real BIC. The landing first appears between tags 0.2.2 and 0.3 and remains in releases beyond the bundle's stated 0.6.2 bound, so there is no patched version boundary or fix commit. First-party design records, the maintainer disposition, and the CNA's rejected record show that possession of the invitation code is intended authentication, making the advisory a false positive rather than an unremediated authentication regression. causal_chain.bug_semantics: The reported mechanism is that POST /api/v1/invitation-code/redeem has no DeveloperDep or API-key dependency and treats an eight-character invitation code as the sole credential; a valid, unexpired, unredeemed code is looked up and exchanged for an SDK-scoped access JWT, a refresh token, and the bound user_id. Thus anyone who obtains a still-valid code can redeem it first. This is not actually missing authentication: the code was deliberately designed as a single-use bearer credential for standalone/mobile onboarding, and the CNA ultimately rejected CVE-2026-78154 as a false positive.
causal_chain.flaw_origin: PR #455 intentionally created the public bearer-code onboarding flow. Its first member commit 8d4ae726e100f72b6687f5a5678f624631c80e8a added backend/app/api/routes/v1/user_invitation_code.py with the public redeem handler and backend/app/services/user_invitation_code_service.py with the code lookup and SDK access/refresh-token issuance. The later squash landing d602dc9f01963e7e7bb9533122dc63368f4d69fd, revocation hardening, async-to-sync refactor, schema move, and documentation clarification did not originate the reported mechanism. The alleged flaw is therefore the original, explicit product design rather than a later accidental authentication regression.

causal_chain.bug_semantics: Because app/mcp/actions.ts begins with the Next.js "use server" directive, its exported async addMcpServer(clientId, config) function is remotely invocable as a Server Action. The function performs no authentication, authorization, or ENABLE_MCP check; it persists the caller-controlled ServerConfig and immediately passes its command, args, and env to initializeSingleClient. That reaches createClient in app/mcp/client.ts, where StdioClientTransport launches the supplied executable when client.connect() runs, yielding unauthenticated remote OS command execution and persistence of the malicious server configuration.

causal_chain.bug_semantics: In non-export deployments, Next.js attaches Access-Control-Allow-Origin: * to every /api/:path* response and, by v2.16.1, also advertises wildcard methods and request headers. An attacker-controlled web origin can therefore read non-credentialed API responses and send normally preflight-restricted headers. In the reported high-impact chain, cross-origin JavaScript supplies x-base-url to the unauthenticated fallback proxy; app/api/proxy.ts builds the server-side destination from that header and injects the configured OpenAI key whenever the supplied value contains api.openai.com, allowing cross-origin SSRF and reflected key disclosure. The invalid Allow-Credentials: true plus wildcard-origin combination does not make credentialed wildcard fetches work in modern browsers, but credentials are unnecessary for the exposed read/proxy path.
causal_chain.flaw_origin: Commit 50cd33dbb2992066dae8c51c2da6ef4781e4500a first created nextConfig.headers for non-export builds and applied Access-Control-Allow-Origin: * (plus Allow-Credentials: true) to /:path*, thereby first granting every web origin read access across the application, including API routes. Its immediate parent had no response-header policy at all. Commit 0fb775d71a0fac5ce4aa802bc3eb0b066c12ed7b then scoped the rule to /api/:path* while widening Allow-Methods and Allow-Headers to * and adding a one-day max age, which intensified the later x-base-url attack but did not originate the permissive-origin flaw. Commit 6f83fbd21278c90cd978108abe54291c38ec10d7 only extracted the unchanged headers into CorsHeaders and is a move/refactor, not the BIC.

Vue then interpreted the returned string through v-html, so merely viewing/searching the shared messages rendered attacker markup and could execute an event-handler payload such as in another user's browser.

causal_chain.bug_semantics: When an administrator runs `fixfiles restore` or the non-full-cleanup path of `fixfiles relabel`, the DEFAULT restore path first has `find` select entries with an unlabeled or undefined SELinux context and then invokes a separate `chcon` process on each pathname. A local attacker controlling a searched directory can replace an intermediate path component with a symlink after `find` checks the entry but before `chcon` resolves the pathname. `chcon --no-dereference` protects only against dereferencing a symlink in the final pathname component; it does not prevent traversal through a swapped intermediate symlink, so the privileged process can change the SELinux label of an arbitrary target such as `/etc/shadow`.
causal_chain.flaw_origin: The vulnerable find-then-chcon mechanism predates the repository's accessible Git history. The earliest relevant Git object, root commit 13cd4c8960688af11ad23b4c946149015c80d549, is explicitly an `initial import from svn trunk revision 2950` and already contains the `/tmp` and `/var/tmp` find/chcon commands. It has no parent and aggregates the prior Subversion history, so it is not the smallest BIC. Later commits changed details without creating the race: 5bd734dd7395a2f6c87546b8e7159b02544405f9 replaced hard-coded label types with `chcon --reference`, and 2608b4d6660af0fb8ad93f2cc144bdaab3c2afa8 added `--no-dereference` but retained the separate pathname lookup. The pre-r2950 Subversion changeset that first introduced the mechanism and its immediate predecessor are not present in the validated clone and could not be reconstructed from the available upstream history.

Line history makes 0b287ed9052f740ecb04df556dd07f03c4186e01 the causal BIC rather than the 2012 helper rename, later refactors, releases, or the unrelated 2026 hardening commit: it adds the packet-reader call path, unchecked length derivation, and over-reading loop together, while its immediate parent has no tcpliveplay.c at all. The BIC is already an ancestor of the specifically affected v4.5.1 release, satisfying the introduction side of the version boundary. No patched side exists because the same mechanism remains in v4.6.1 and current HEAD, so null fix SHAs are justified as unpatched rather than unknown. causal_chain.bug_semantics: A crafted Juniper-Ethernet pcap can advertise unsupported extension media/encapsulation while still being long enough for dlt_jnpr_ether_decode() to treat the post-extension bytes as Ethernet. A successful en10mb subdecoder decode is followed by tcpedit_dlt_copy_decoder_state(), which assigns the subcontext-owned decoded_extra allocation directly to the outer context. Cleanup then traverses the outer context and the recursively owned subcontext; dlt_linuxsll2_cleanup() frees each context's decoded_extra pointer, so the aliased allocation is freed twice and tcprewrite aborts or corrupts memory.
causal_chain.flaw_origin: Commit 745a71184c9d739305d4319cf2e6bb3998cc27b6 introduced the Juniper subdecoder lifecycle as one cohesive feature: it created an en10mb subcontext, copied subdecoder state by borrowing the decoded_extra pointer without transferring or recording ownership, and recursively destroyed the subcontext during outer cleanup. It also continued to decode Juniper payloads as Ethernet without validating the extension-declared media type and encapsulation. Those combined lines first created the aliased-ownership double-free path; later aggregate/import commit 77387f1580220c1232a9091c79d0db83ba7ac5b0 merely reintroduced the already-existing mechanism into the 4.0 line.

causal_chain.bug_semantics: The REST frontend registered an /engine-ui proxy whose request path supplied both the destination host and port. EngineUIProxyServlet parsed /engine-ui/<host>:<port>/..., then constructed and issued an HTTP request to that destination without an enable/disable gate or destination allowlist. A remote requester able to reach the proxy could therefore make the Kyuubi server contact arbitrary hosts reachable from the server, yielding SSRF/open-proxy behavior.

causal_chain.bug_semantics: AIT CSV Import/Export through 3.0.3 exposed admin/upload-handler.php as a directly reachable unauthenticated multipart upload endpoint. It neither restricted the uploaded file to safe CSV content/types nor prevented a PHP filename from being placed in WordPress's web-executable wp-content/uploads directory. causal_chain.bug_semantics: ClassroomIO treated email-verification state and token contents as client authority. The profile table's existing own-row UPDATE policy allowed an authenticated user to set the newly added is_email_verified column directly through PostgREST. Independently, the emailed verification value was only Base64-encoded JSON containing a client-selected profileId and orgSiteName; /api/verify decoded it without a signature, expiry, one-time-use check, authenticated-user binding, or ownership check and used profileId in a privileged profile update. An attacker could therefore self-verify through the profile API or forge data for the verification endpoint to mark a chosen profile verified without controlling its mailbox.
causal_chain.flaw_origin: PR #215's first member commit, 69ba4c1a23504004f9d888312916862fb93003bf, created the verification-email route, the /api/verify route, and the profile verification columns. It first wrote both the unsigned btoa(JSON.stringify({ profileId, orgSiteName })) token construction and the unvalidated profile update, while the pre-existing policy "Users can update own profile." permitted an authenticated owner to update all profile columns. Member 947cfc06ca3a858972e8faafd096c7f662ef6086 later changed /api/verify to getServerSupabase, completing the arbitrary-profile service-role attack path, but it retained rather than originated the client-authoritative token and update mechanism. GitHub squash bd905b580a203309e244db16b06187c5103924cc landed the reconstructed member series on main.

causal_chain.bug_semantics: An authenticated Contributor who can create or edit a mep_events post can store quote-bearing payloads in event address fields (venue, street, city, state, postcode, and country) and related configurable registration labels. Those stored values were subsequently returned from post/term metadata and inserted without escaping into single-quoted HTML value attributes and Google Maps iframe URLs (and labels into attribute contexts), so a quote could terminate the attribute and add an event handler that executes when a privileged user or visitor renders the affected event/admin page.

The application treats client-side navigation hiding and Svelte RoleBasedSecurity rendering/redirects as authorization, while route scripts and data services still execute course-ID-keyed reads without enforcing a tutor/admin role at the data boundary. As a result, all-course member profiles, attendance, submissions and answers, marks, and analytics can be returned before the client hides the slot or redirects, producing the advisory's transient sensitive-data disclosure.

Decomposing Lucee's 2015 root import back into those Railo snapshots reaches the earliest public boundary but not the original authoring commit. reasoning: The vulnerability requires the realloc transition, not get_l2len_protocol itself: that parser is merely the observed stale-pointer consumer. History proves 69831b8186513309f4dd43ca5bacfc34b554ad14 is the atomic commit that first introduced realloc into the --fixlen pad branch while tcpedit_packet retained aliases established before the call. Its immediate parent cannot free or move pktdata on this path, establishing parent absence. Later commits changed pointer propagation and allocation headroom without removing the stale-alias hazard, and the flaw remained in every checked release from v4.0.5 through v4.5.1/v4.5.2-beta2. Commit 73008f261f1cdf7a1087dc8759115242696d35da fixes the root by eliminating the realloc and bounding wire length to the preallocated capacity, with its own version metadata marking 4.5.2-beta3 and the v4.5.2 tag containing it. The BIC is a normal single-parent commit, not a merge/squash/backport, so no decomposition is applicable. Finally, the BIC commit object has a human author/committer and no AI marker; under the required BIC-only attribution rule, the closed verdict is NOT_AI.

causal_chain.bug_semantics: A locally supplied truncated pcap (wire length greater than captured length) processed by tcprewrite --fixlen pad reaches untrunc_packet, which reallocates the packet buffer and may free its old address. tcpedit_packet has already cached packet and IP-header aliases into that old allocation and does not rebase them after untrunc_packet returns; its later DLT merge path calls dlt_en10mb_l2len/get_l2len/get_l2len_protocol through the stale packet address, producing the reported heap use-after-free read (and other post-padding paths could likewise use stale header aliases).
causal_chain.flaw_origin: Commit 69831b8186513309f4dd43ca5bacfc34b554ad14 changed untrunc_packet from padding the caller-provided buffer in place to safe_realloc(packet, pkthdr->len), and changed the API/caller to pass u_char **pktdata, but tcpedit_packet continued retaining its pre-call local packet, ip_hdr, and ip6_hdr aliases. In that original commit untrunc_packet did not even assign the new packet back through *pktdata; b58b23a52ffd23c3b1a2e2fe8b868aff0239560d later added *pktdata = packet but still did not rebase tcpedit_packet's cached aliases, so it did not cure the causal stale-pointer mechanism. The smallest first-writer is therefore 69831b8186513309f4dd43ca5bacfc34b554ad14, not the later headroom adjustment 64132c54c4000046b30f1fc3fe612db9b2f26860.

ICTBroadcast passes the attacker-controlled session identifier into a shell-backed session-log command of the form sh -c echo "... Session read requested with id: <cookie> ..." >> gui.log. Because the cookie is not shell-neutralized, the shell evaluates the embedded backticks; a payload that base64-decodes and pipes a command to sh therefore executes arbitrary commands as the web-service account before authentication.

The profile flow uploaded the supplied bytes unchanged to the public Supabase avatars bucket, merely naming the object with a .webp suffix, then persisted its public URL.
